request: Why are most published research findings false? Show the base-rate arithmetic, and put the paper itself on the slide: https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.0020124
title: Most findings are false

spec.title: Why most published findings are false

elements.of: Why Most Published Research Findings Are False

commands.speak: Take a thousand hypotheses a field might test in a year.
Each one is either really true or really false — and the study either reaches significance or it does not.
Suppose a hundred of the thousand are genuinely true. That is a generous field.
A study with eighty per cent power finds eighty of those hundred, and misses twenty.
Of the nine hundred false hypotheses, a five per cent significance threshold still hands back forty-five significant results.
So a hundred and twenty-five papers report a significant finding — and forty-five of them, more than one in three, are false.
John Ioannidis made exactly this arithmetic famous in 2005; his paper is linked here.
Nothing was fabricated and no rule was broken. The false-discovery rate falls straight out of the base rate, the power, and the threshold.

request: What can attention do that recurrence could not? Quote the paper's own sentence for it: https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762
title: Attention, in the paper's words

elements.quote: dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely

commands.speak: What could attention do that recurrence couldn't? Take a sentence: 'Anna told Ben she left.' To understand 'she', a network must find Anna.
A recurrent network reads in order, carrying a running memory from word to word. Anna reaches 'she' only by passing through 'told' and 'Ben'.
And each step waits for the one before, so a thousand-word text is a thousand steps in a row that no chip can share out.
Attention drops the queue: 'she' looks directly at the other words and scores how relevant each one is.
Anna scores highest, so her meaning flows straight into 'she': one hop, however far back she was named.
Every word does this at the same time, so the whole sentence is computed in one parallel pass instead of a queue.
The 2017 paper that made this the standard design said it in one line of its abstract:
dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely.
Attention itself wasn't new: it already helped recurrent translators. The bold step was removing the recurrence around it.
The payoff was speed. The paper's largest model trained in three and a half days on eight GPUs, and its design became the T in GPT.
So the gift was less attention than parallelism: a model that reads a whole text at once can learn from vastly more of it.

quiz.question: What did dropping recurrence buy the Transformer, above all?
choices: Every word processed at once, in parallel
Attention, which did not exist before
quiz.right: Parallelism: with no word-by-word queue, every position is computed at the same time, so training on huge amounts of text became fast.

request: Why did Malthus think population growth must end in famine, and was he right?
title: Malthus's two lines

elements.of: An Essay on the Principle of Population

commands.speak: In 1798 Thomas Malthus argued that famine was not bad luck but arithmetic. Was he right? His Essay on the Principle of Population rests on two lines.
People grow by multiplication. The American colonies had been doubling every twenty-five years: two, four, eight, sixteen.
Food, he argued, grows only by addition: clear another field, drain another marsh. The same amount more each generation.
Start them level, and the gap opens and never closes. Everyone above the food line must go without.
After a century, sixteen times the people and five times the food. After two, his own figures: 256 to 9.
Any doubling, however slow, overtakes any straight line, however steep. So famine, or late marriage and fewer births, had to hold people back.
The arithmetic holds. What broke was the straight line.
Fertiliser, new crops and machines made food multiply too, and faster than people.
Since 1800 the world has grown from one billion people to eight, and food per head has still gone up.
His other line bent as well: as people grew richer, they chose smaller families, and world population growth has been slowing since the late 1960s.
The essay had one reader Malthus never expected: in 1838 Charles Darwin read it, and saw in its struggle for food the engine of natural selection.

quiz.question: Suppose food rose by twice as much each generation, still by addition. Would that avoid Malthus's gap forever?
quiz.right: No: a steeper straight line only moves the crossing later, because a doubling curve overtakes any line. Only food that multiplies keeps up.

request: What is a derivative, really? Link Grant Sanderson's calculus video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WUvTyaaNkzM
title: The derivative is a limit of slopes

commands.speak: A derivative is the rate of change at one instant — which sounds impossible. Take a dropped stone: after t seconds it has fallen five t squared metres.
Two seconds in, it has fallen twenty metres. How fast is it moving at exactly that moment?
Speed needs two moments. At four seconds it has fallen eighty metres, and the line through both points has a slope…
…of sixty metres fallen over two seconds…
…which is thirty metres a second, on average.
But the stone kept speeding up after two seconds, so thirty is too fast for the moment we asked about.
Close the gap to one second: twenty-five metres more, so twenty-five metres a second.
Shrink it further — a tenth, a hundredth of a second — and the slope stops changing, closing in on twenty.
That limit is the derivative: twenty metres a second, the slope of the tangent — the line that just grazes the curve at two seconds.
Why not set the gap to zero? Then the stone falls zero metres in zero seconds, and zero over zero says nothing.
So the derivative is not a slope measured at one point, but the number the slopes head for as the gap shrinks.
A speedometer shows exactly this: never distance over a whole trip, only where that ratio is heading right now.
Newton wrote a dot over the letter, Leibniz wrote d y over d x, and this prime is Lagrange's — three names for one limit.
Click this label for Grant Sanderson's video, which builds the same limit from scratch.

quiz.question: From 2 s to 4 s the stone averages 30 m/s. Its speed at exactly 2 s is…
choices: zero — an instant has no speed
quiz.right: Less — twenty metres a second: the stone speeds up, so any stretch after two seconds averages more than its speed at two.

request: A disease hits 1 in 10,000. The test catches 90% of cases and false-alarms only 1% of the time. I tested positive — should I panic? Add 3Blue1Brown's Bayes video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HZGCoVF3YvM
title: Positive on a very good test

spec.title: A very good test, a very rare disease

card.title: A good test, a rare disease

commands.speak: Should a positive on a very good test make you panic? It depends on how rare the disease is. Follow a hundred thousand people instead of percentages.
The disease hits one in ten thousand: ten of them have it, and ninety-nine thousand nine hundred and ninety do not.
The test catches ninety percent of real cases: nine of the ten test positive, and one is missed.
It false-alarms one time in a hundred. Small — but one percent of almost a hundred thousand is a thousand people.
A thousand healthy people are told they might be sick.
Everyone with a positive result stands in one of these two boxes: nine sick, a thousand healthy.
So a positive puts you among one thousand and nine people, of whom nine are sick. Under one percent.
The test didn't fail. Your chance rose about ninety-fold, from one in ten thousand to nearly one in a hundred. It just started very low.
Now say you went to the doctor with symptoms, and one in a hundred people like you has the disease. Same test.
Nine hundred true positives now face nine hundred and ninety false ones. The same positive means nearly even odds.
Back to one in ten thousand. What a positive result means depends on who takes the test.
When Gerd Gigerenzer gave doctors counts like these instead of percentages, far more of them got this question right.
Click this label for 3Blue1Brown's picture of why.

quiz.question: With this 1-in-10,000 disease, you test positive on two independent tests. Roughly what is your chance now?
quiz.right: Close to half: after one positive you are one of 1,009 with nine sick; a second test keeps about eight of them against ten false alarms.

request: How can a drug help every group of patients yet look harmful overall? Link the article: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simpson%27s_paradox
title: When the trend reverses

commands.speak: How can a drug help every group of patients, yet look harmful when you add them up? That's Simpson's paradox. Here, ten patients: dose against recovery.
Five mild cases got low doses. Among them, every extra ten milligrams bought about four points of recovery.
Five severe cases got high doses. They start lower, because they are sicker, but gain the same four points per ten milligrams.
Now ignore who was sick and fit one line through all ten. It slopes down: more drug, worse recovery.
Nothing in the data changed. This line compares low-dose mild patients with high-dose severe ones.
The drop from one cloud to the other is severity, not dose. Doctors gave the sickest the most drug, and the pooled line blames the drug.
Which to believe? The numbers can't say. The story of how doses were chosen says compare like with like: within each group, the drug helps.
It happens with real data: in a 1986 study of kidney-stone surgery, open surgery did better on small stones and on large ones, yet worse overall.
It had been given more of the hard cases. Click the pooled line for the article.
An average over a mix of patients answers a question about the mix, not about the drug.

quiz.question: Sicker patients get more of a drug, and pooled data show high doses doing worse. What should you check first?
choices: The dose effect within each severity group
Whether the pooled line is steep
quiz.right: Compare like with like: within each severity group, higher doses did better. The pooled slope mixes the drug's effect with how sick people were.

request: How can two sounds add up to silence? Put 3Blue1Brown's Fourier video on the slide: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=spUNpyF58BY
title: Waves that cancel

card.title: How can two sounds make silence?

commands.speak: How can two sounds add up to silence? Noise-cancelling headphones do it. Here is a steady hum: air pressure rising and falling, a hundred times a second.
The headphones play a second wave of their own. Suppose it is an exact copy, in step with the hum.
Sound waves add point by point: crest on crest, trough on trough. The sum swings twice as far — louder, not quieter.
Now delay the copy by half a wave. For a hundred-hertz hum that is five thousandths of a second.
Every crest now meets a trough of the same size, and the sum is flat: the air at your ear barely moves.
Here the hum pushes the air up, and at the same instant the copy pulls it down by exactly as much.
Real headphones flip the sound upside down rather than delay it: a microphone hears the hum, and the speaker plays its mirror image.
That works best on steady, low sounds like an engine's drone — a voice changes too fast to be matched in time.
Any sound is a sum of simple waves like these — Fourier's idea. 3Blue1Brown's video shows how to take a sound apart into them.
Click the still to watch it.

quiz.question: A delay of 5 thousandths of a second silences a 100 Hz hum. What does the same delay do to a 200 Hz hum?
quiz.right: Louder: at 200 hertz, five thousandths of a second is a whole wave, so crest lands on crest again.

commands.speak: How many random draws before their average can be trusted? This Python simulation runs for real, in your browser.
Two knobs: how many draws to take, and a button that throws a fresh batch.
Every draw comes from a bell curve centred on zero, so the true average is exactly zero.
The script prints the sample's average, the number we hope lands on zero.
Beside it, how far such an average typically misses: one over the square root of the number of draws.
Then a histogram of the draws, with the true bell curve drawn over it to compare.
Two hundred draws: the average is 0.016, and the typical miss is 0.071. This batch landed closer than most.
Now twenty draws, then two hundred, then two thousand. The typical miss falls from 0.22 to 0.07 to 0.02.
A hundred times the draws bought only ten times the precision. The miss shrinks with the square root, not with the count.
That the average must settle at all was proved by Jacob Bernoulli; his proof appeared in 1713, eight years after his death.
Drag the draws yourself and press Draw again: at twenty the average jumps about, at two thousand it barely stirs.

quiz.question: An average of 500 draws typically misses by 0.045. How many draws to halve that miss?
quiz.right: Two thousand: the miss shrinks with the square root of the draws, so halving it takes four times as many.

commands.speak: How close to half should five hundred flips of a fair coin land? This Python script flips them for real, right in your browser.
Two hundred and forty-nine heads: a share of 0.498. Almost exactly half, but not quite.
On a ruler from 0.40 to 0.60, our coin lands a hair left of the middle.
Landing exactly on half is not even likely: the script puts the chance of precisely 250 heads under four percent.
What is normal is a wobble of about 0.022 either way. Nineteen fair coins in twenty land inside this band, 0.455 to 0.545.
Three hundred heads would sit at 0.60, far outside it. That coin you should stop trusting.
The band narrows with more flips. Interned in Denmark in the war, John Kerrich flipped a coin ten thousand times and got 5,067 heads.
So a fair coin is not one that lands on half. It is one that lands inside the band.

quiz.question: A coin gives 270 heads in 500 flips, a share of 0.54. Is that proof it's biased?
choices: No: it's still inside the band
quiz.right: No: 0.54 is still inside the band where nineteen fair coins in twenty land, so 500 flips cannot convict it.

commands.speak: Why does compound growth curve upward when the rate never changes? A hundred dollars over fifty years, computed in Python.
Two rates, two percent and seven, and the same chart drawn twice.
The only difference between the two charts is how the vertical axis is ruled.
Then the two totals, and what seven percent earns in the first year and in the last.
On an ordinary axis, two percent looks almost straight, and seven percent bends sharply upward.
Two hundred and sixty-nine against 2,946. And the yearly gain grows from seven dollars to a hundred and ninety-three.
That is the bend: seven percent every year, but of an ever bigger pile. Each year's gain is proportional to what is already there.
Now rule the axis by multiples instead: each gridline ten times the one below.
Both curves turn into straight lines. A steady percentage is a steady slope; seven percent just climbs steeper.
So the rate never speeds up. The bend is what steady percentage growth looks like on an axis that counts in dollars.
Logarithms, which John Napier published in 1614, turn multiplying into adding. That is exactly what this axis does to growth.

quiz.question: On a log-scale chart, how does a fund growing a steady 7 % a year look?
quiz.right: A straight line: each year multiplies by the same 1.07, and on a log axis equal multiples are equal steps.

request: Why do the primes thin out? Count them in Python below 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50, adding the bars as you go

elements.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
def is_prime(k):
    divisors = range(2, int(k ** 0.5) + 1)
    return k > 1 and all(k % d for d in divisors)
limits = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]
counts = [sum(is_prime(k) for k in range(n)) for n in limits]
for stage in (2, 4, 5):
    plt.figure()
    plt.bar([str(n) for n in limits[:stage]], counts[:stage])
    plt.xlim(-0.6, 4.6)
    plt.ylim(0, 16)
print("share below 50:", counts[-1] / 50)

request: Why does averaging dice produce a bell curve?

spec.title: Where the bell curve comes from

elements.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
edges = np.linspace(1, 6, 12)
def shares(n):
    means = rng.integers(1, 7, size=(20000, n)).mean(axis=1)
    counts, _ = np.histogram(means, bins=edges)
    return [round(float(c) / 20000, 3) for c in counts]
frames = [shares(1), shares(2), shares(10)]

card.title: Where the bell curve comes from

commands.speak: Why does the bell curve turn up everywhere, even from dice? Roll one die twenty thousand times: each face comes up a sixth of the time.
Six equal spikes. Nothing about one die is bell-shaped.
Now roll two dice and plot their average. The half-steps fill in, and the middle rises.
An average of one needs a double one: one way out of thirty-six.
An average of three and a half has six ways: one and six, two and five, three and four, each either way round.
Average ten dice, and the triangle melts into a bell.
It narrows too. An extreme average needs all ten dice to agree, and that almost never happens.
A third of all averages now land in this one middle bar.
Abraham de Moivre found this curve in 1733, counting heads in long runs of coin tosses.
The dice never changed: each still shows any face a sixth of the time. The bell belongs to the average, not the die.
That is the central limit theorem: add many independent bits of chance, and a bell appears whatever each bit looked like.

quiz.question: After averaging ten dice thousands of times, what is the chance a single die shows a six?
quiz.right: Still one in six: each die is as flat as ever. Only the average of many dice is bell-shaped.

commands.speak: How can a treatment win in every group yet lose overall? Kidney-stone data from a 1986 British study: open surgery, A, against a keyhole method, B.
Overall, B wins: eighty-three percent of its patients treated successfully, against seventy-eight for A.
Now split the same patients by stone size. On small stones, A wins: ninety-three percent against eighty-seven.
On large stones, A wins again: seventy-three against sixty-nine. Better in both groups, worse in total.
The answer is in the counts. Three quarters of A's patients had large stones; under a quarter of B's did.

Each total is an average of the two rows, weighted by how many patients sit in each. Here is A's.
Three quarters of the weight falls on large stones, so A's total is dragged down towards seventy-three. B's leans the other way, towards eighty-seven.
So the totals compare the mix of patients as much as the treatments. The rows compare like with like.
Edward Simpson described the effect in 1951, but Udny Yule had spotted it about fifty years earlier.

quiz.question: If each treatment had been given to equal numbers of small and large stones, which would have done better overall?
quiz.right: A: half and half gives A about eighty-three percent and B about seventy-eight. With the mix equal, winning in each group wins overall.

The median only asks who stands in the middle. The mean adds up every dollar, so the few big incomes drag it to the right.
Add random amounts instead of multiplying, and the bell stays symmetric: mean and median sit together, and half earn below average.
In 1931 the French engineer Robert Gibrat argued that growth in proportion to size makes incomes and firms lopsided in just this way.
So below average is where most people are, wherever luck comes as percentages.

quiz.question: In a lopsided income distribution like this one, what share of people earn less than the average?
quiz.right: More than half: the few large incomes in the tail pull the mean above the median, and the median is where half the people are.

A small bakery's week, in made-up numbers: six items, a thousand dollars of sales, listed alphabetically.
Into a table, one row per item.
Each item's share of the week: its sales divided by the total.
Then sort from the best seller down. The alphabet hid the pattern; this order asks where the money comes from.
A running share adds the shares as we go down the list: how much of the week do the top items bring?
Print the table, and chart the shares as bars.
Cake alone is half the sales. Cake and pies together, two items of six, bring in seventy-five percent.
The other four, two thirds of the menu, share the last quarter. Tarts bring three percent.
If every item pulled equal weight, each bar would stand at seventeen percent, and the running share would climb in even steps.
Joseph Juran called this lopsidedness the Pareto principle, after Vilfredo Pareto, who found most of Italy's land owned by a small share of its people.
Sort, then add up: two lines of pandas find where the weight sits in any list.

quiz.question: Four of the six items are two thirds of the menu. What share of the week's sales do they bring?
quiz.right: About a quarter: the running share is already 0.75 after cake and pies, so the other four together bring the last 0.25.

commands.speak: If interest is added more and more often, does money grow without limit? One dollar at a hundred percent a year, in a Python of half a megabyte.
Split the year into n pieces: once, twice, quarterly, monthly, weekly, daily.
Each piece earns a hundred percent divided by n, and each piece's interest earns interest in all the pieces after it.
Print what the dollar has become by the end of the year.
The last line is left bare, so its value shows: a number we will need in a moment.
Once a year, the dollar becomes two. Twice a year, 2.25. Monthly, 2.61. Daily, 2.7146.
Each step gains less than the one before. Going from monthly to daily, thirty times as often, adds barely ten cents.
The tempting guess is that twice as often means twice the bonus, without end. Instead the gains shrink towards a ceiling.
The ceiling is e, 2.71828. Interest added every instant still turns one dollar into less than 2.72.
More pieces mean more interest on interest, but each piece earns less; the two effects balance ever more closely, and the total levels off.
Jacob Bernoulli asked this very question about a sum lent at full interest in 1683, and so found the number now called e.
At five percent a year, daily adding pays 5.13 percent instead of 5: the rate matters far more than how often it is added.

quiz.question: A bank adds the 100 % interest every second instead of every day. What does the dollar become in a year?
quiz.right: About 2.72: daily adding already reaches 2.7146, and every second only closes the last cents to the ceiling, e.

commands.speak: Why does a test at five percent reject beyond 1.96 standard errors, and not some other number? This curve is what chance alone produces.
It is centred on zero, the result a treatment with no effect would give on average.
Each rung is one standard error: how far a result wobbles by chance alone.
The test sets aside the five percent of results least likely under no effect. Two-sided, that five percent is split: 2.5 in each tail.
Python's inverse normal found the point with exactly 2.5 percent beyond it: 1.96 standard errors.
Put all five percent in the right tail instead, and the cutoff moves in, to 1.645. A one-sided test is easier to pass.
So a result 1.8 standard errors above zero passes the one-sided test and fails the two-sided one. Same data, different verdict.
That is why the side is chosen before the data arrive. Picking it after seeing which way the result fell doubles the false alarms, to ten percent.
Two-sided, the cutoff stays at 1.96.
The same 1.96 builds the 95 percent confidence interval, estimate plus or minus 1.96 standard errors. The test rejects exactly when that interval misses zero.
Abraham de Moivre found this curve in 1733, as a shortcut for adding up the chances of long runs of coin tosses.

quiz.right: Only one-sided, chosen in advance: 1.8 clears the one-tail cutoff of 1.645, but not 1.96, where a two-sided test splits its five percent.

request: What should a meta-analysis do when its trials disagree? Four trials pooled in Python, with and without random effects

elements.code:
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import chi2
est = np.array([0.82, 0.71, 1.12, 0.55])
lo = np.array([0.63, 0.55, 0.90, 0.42])
hi = np.array([1.07, 0.92, 1.39, 0.72])
y = np.log(est)
se = (np.log(hi) - np.log(lo)) / (2 * 1.96)
w = 1 / se ** 2
fixed = (w * y).sum() / w.sum()
q = (w * (y - fixed) ** 2).sum()
df = len(y) - 1
p_het = round(float(chi2.sf(q, df)), 4)
i2 = round(max(0.0, (q - df) / q), 2)
tau2 = max(0.0, (q - df) / (w.sum() - (w ** 2).sum() / w.sum()))
wr = 1 / (se ** 2 + tau2)
mu = (wr * y).sum() / wr.sum()
half = 1.96 / np.sqrt(wr.sum())
pooled = {k: round(float(np.exp(v)), 3) for k, v in
          [("est", mu), ("lo", mu - half), ("hi", mu + half)]}

commands.speak: A meta-analysis pools trials into one estimate. But what if the trials disagree? Four trials of a drug against relapse; a risk ratio below 1 means it helps.
Anderson finds 0.82 and Bianchi 0.71: both lean towards benefit.
Carter finds 1.12: if anything, more relapses on the drug.
Diallo finds 0.55, a large benefit. Its interval and Carter's do not even overlap.
The simple pooled average, weighting each trial by its precision, gives 0.81, from 0.71 to 0.91: a confident benefit.
But that average assumes one true effect, with trials differing only by chance. Trials this far apart would arise by chance less than once in a thousand.
The measure I-squared puts it in one number: eighty-three percent of the spread between these trials is real difference, not noise.
So Python pools with random effects: each trial has its own true effect, and the diamond estimates their average: 0.78, from 0.58 to 1.05.
The diamond is wider, and it now crosses 1. The confident answer came from pretending the trials agreed.
The better question is no longer the average, but why Carter and Diallo differ: other patients, other doses, other follow-up.
I-squared is young: Julian Higgins and Simon Thompson proposed it in 2002, and most meta-analyses now report it.

quiz.question: The trials disagree far more than chance allows. How does the random-effects diamond compare with the fixed-effect one?
quiz.right: Wider: it must cover how much the true effect varies from trial to trial, not only each trial's sampling error.

commands.speak: How much longer does a treatment keep patients alive? Trials usually answer with the median, and sometimes the median cannot be found. One trial, month by month.
Standard care: 118 patients. Eighteen die in month one, twenty in month two; after five months forty-four are alive, thirty-seven percent.
Treatment: 120 patients and fewer deaths every month. After five months seventy-seven are alive, sixty-four percent.
Median survival is where a curve falls to one half. On standard care that happens in month four.
The treated curve never gets there: most are still alive when follow-up ends. The report says 'median not reached', and the comparison has no number.
The area under each curve still gives one. It counts the months lived, on average, within the five months followed.
Under standard care, 3.5 of the first five months. Under treatment, 4.2.
The shaded gap between the staircases is the gain: two-thirds of a month per patient, about three weeks, on average.
A median reads one height on one curve. The area uses every month, so early deaths and late ones all count.
Its name is the restricted mean survival time: restricted, because it stops where follow-up stops, and says nothing about month six.
Told in 1982 that his cancer's median survival was eight months, Stephen Jay Gould wrote 'The Median Isn't the Message'. He lived twenty more years.

quiz.question: Two drugs have the same median survival, 12 months. Can their mean survival differ?
choices: No, same median means same survival
Yes, the areas under the curves can differ
Only if the trials differ in size
quiz.right: Yes: the median reads one point on each curve, while the area adds up every month, so what happens before and after the halfway point still counts.

request: Why is a cost-effectiveness acceptability curve a slope and not a yes-or-no?

commands.speak: Why is an acceptability curve a gentle slope, not a yes or no? Along the bottom: what we would pay for one QALY, in thousands of dollars.
Suppose we knew a new drug adds exactly 0.22 QALYs for 9,000 dollars more. Then the answer would be a step.
Nine thousand over 0.22 is about forty-one thousand per QALY, the ICER. Below it the drug never pays its way; above it, it always does.
But both numbers are uncertain. The script draws four thousand plausible pairs, cost give or take 3,000, gain give or take 0.09, and at each price counts the drug's wins.
Standard care is the mirror image: in every draw, exactly one of the two comes out ahead.
The step has been smeared into a slope, centred where the step stood. How wide the smear is, is how much we don't know.
At thirty thousand the step said never. Yet the drug wins in just over a quarter of the draws: those where it works better than the mean.
At fifty thousand the step said always, and the drug wins in only about two draws of three.
So the curve holds two things at once: where the ICER lies, and how sure we are of it.
Pinning that second thing down is why England's NICE has asked for probabilistic analysis like this since its 2004 methods guide.

quiz.question: A larger trial halves the uncertainty about the drug's effect. At $30,000 per QALY, the chance it is cost-effective…
quiz.right: It falls. Less uncertainty steepens the curve around the same crossing, near forty-one thousand, so below it the drug wins in fewer draws.

commands.speak: Did New Jersey's minimum-wage rise, from $4.25 to $5.05 in April 1992, cost jobs? Difference-in-differences answers by comparing with a neighbour that stood still.
Card and Krueger surveyed fast-food restaurants in February and again in November. In New Jersey, jobs per restaurant went from 20.44 to 21.03.
Jobs means full-time equivalents: full-timers and managers, plus half of each part-timer.
Across the river, eastern Pennsylvania kept its minimum at $4.25. Its restaurants went from 23.33 to 21.17.
Pennsylvania starting higher does not matter: the method compares changes, not levels.
The step to see: had New Jersey changed as Pennsylvania did, it would have fallen 2.16, to 18.28. That third line is borrowed, never observed.
What happened minus what would have: 21.03 minus 18.28, about 2.75 more jobs per restaurant. Not fewer.
Now split that 2.75. New Jersey's own change was only 0.59.
The other 2.16 is Pennsylvania's fall. Most of the estimate comes from the comparison state, so the result rests on believing New Jersey would have fallen too.
That is why the study was fought over for years, with payroll records and new data. It changed how economists argue about minimum wages.
David Card shared the 2021 Nobel prize partly for this work. Alan Krueger, his co-author, had died two years earlier.

quiz.question: Suppose Pennsylvania had held steady at 23.33 jobs per restaurant. What would the estimate be?
quiz.right: +0.59: with a flat comparison, the estimate is just New Jersey's own change. The comparison state's path is half of every difference-in-differences.

commands.speak: Why estimate a reform's effect quarter by quarter, rather than as one before-and-after number? The quarter-by-quarter picture is an event study.
Take a simulated reform: forty hospitals start caring for frail patients at home, each compared with a similar hospital that does not.
Each dot is the gap in emergency admissions per thousand residents, against the quarter just before the reform. Before it, the gaps sit on zero.
The script fits a line through them too: a slope of almost nothing, so the comparison hospitals were moving in step.
In the first quarter after the reform, admissions fall by about half a case per thousand.
Then more each quarter, to nearly two by the fifth. The whiskers, from the script's standard errors, stay well clear of zero.
And the effect is still growing when the data stop.
One before-and-after number averages these five: about 1.2. That is neither where the effect started nor where it ended up.
Worse, it depends on when you stop looking. Two quarters of data would have said 0.7.
When reforms start at different dates and effects grow like this, the usual pooled regression can even get the sign wrong, as Andrew Goodman-Bacon showed in 2021.
So an event study answers two questions a single number merges: was there an effect, and how did it unfold?

quiz.question: A reform's effect grows every quarter. If you pool two years of data instead of one, the single before-and-after estimate will be…
quiz.right: Larger. A pooled number averages a growing effect, so a longer window takes in the bigger later quarters; the quarter-by-quarter dots stay where they are.

request: Why does an epidemic wave turn around before everyone is infected? An SIR model in R

sir <- function(r0, days = 250, gamma = 0.1) {
  s <- 0.999; i <- 0.001
  S <- I <- numeric(days)
  for (d in seq_len(days)) {
    S[d] <- round(s, 4); I[d] <- round(i, 4)
    new <- r0 * gamma * s * i
    s <- s - new
    i <- i + new - gamma * i
  }
  list(S = S, I = I)
}

commands.speak: Why does an epidemic wave turn around while many people are still uninfected? A model in R: almost everyone starts susceptible, one in a thousand ill.
Each day, new infections are made where the ill meet the susceptible…
…so they grow with both shares at once: fewer susceptibles, fewer new cases, however many are ill.
And a tenth of the ill recover each day, leaving the game.
Run it for 250 days with each case infecting 2.5 others, then with 1.4.
The susceptible share falls, fast at first, as the virus uses people up.
The ill share rises into a wave that peaks on day 51, with nearly a quarter ill at once.
Read the two lines together: at the peak, the susceptible share has fallen to forty percent.
That is one over 2.5. Each case now meets so few susceptibles that it infects exactly one other: fewer than one, and the wave must shrink.
At 1.4 the wave turns much earlier, while seventy-one percent are still susceptible: one over 1.4.
A wave ends not because the virus weakens, but because each case finds too few people left to infect.
Kermack and McKendrick published this model in 1927, with this threshold at its heart.

quiz.question: A virus spreads with each case infecting 4 others. At what susceptible share does its wave peak?
quiz.right: Twenty-five percent: one over four. Below that, each case infects fewer than one other, so the wave shrinks.

Each is built to grow about six centimetres a year, plus a few centimetres of individual difference.
Here they are: a tight, rising cloud, from 87 centimetres at two to 148 at twelve.
lm finds the line that makes the squared vertical gaps from the dots as small as possible.
coef hands its slope and intercept to the chart.
6.29 centimetres a year. Inside the data it is superb: it accounts for 98 percent of the spread.
But the axis runs on to age thirty-two, and the line runs with it. Nothing in it knows where the data stopped.
Now one grown-up, left out of the fit: 170 centimetres at thirty.
The adult lands far below the line.
At thirty the line says 263. It is off by almost a metre, though it fitted the children nearly perfectly.
It fails backwards too: at age zero it says 74.5 centimetres, where a newborn is about 50.
Forwards, by about thirty-one it passes 2.72 metres, the height of Robert Wadlow, the tallest person on record.

card.title: How many draws make a bell

commands.speak: Why does a histogram of a hundred random draws look so lumpy, and how many draws does it take to show the bell they came from?
First the true bell itself, computed point by point, so every histogram has the right answer drawn over it.
Two sample sizes, a hundred and ten thousand, both drawn from that same bell.
Each gets its own histogram. Density scaling puts both on one scale, so their shapes can be compared directly.
The bell on top, fixed axes, a title, and show it: two figures from one script.
A hundred draws: ragged bars, some well above the curve, some well below. Yet every one of them came from a perfect bell.
A bar that should hold ten draws typically gets seven to thirteen: chance moves it by about a third of its height.
Ten thousand draws, and the bars hug the curve.
A bar that should hold a thousand gets between 970 and 1030: three percent. A hundred times the data, ten times smoother.
The wobble shrinks with the square root of the count, not with the count: to halve it, you need four times the draws.
The same square root sets a poll's margin: a thousand people give about three points either way, whatever the size of the country.
So a lumpy small sample is no evidence against the bell: a shape can only be judged once there are draws enough to show it.

quiz.question: To make each bar's chance wobble half as big, how many draws do you need?
quiz.right: Four times as many: the wobble shrinks with the square root of the count, and the square root of four is two.

commands.speak: Why do neighbouring Fibonacci numbers settle into one odd ratio, 1.618? Two ones to start, in MicroPython, a Python small enough for a microcontroller.
Each step slides the pair along: one and two, two and three, three and five, the new number always the sum of the last two.
And it records the new number divided by the one before.
The ratios: two, then one and a half, 1.67, 1.6, 1.625. They jump above and below, closing in.
Mind the axis: it starts at 1.4, not zero, so the wobble looks big. By the tenth step it is in the fourth decimal.
Why the zigzag? The next ratio is b plus a, over b: one plus one over the last ratio.
A ratio that is too big makes one over it too small, so the next ratio undershoots, and each miss is smaller than the last.
The zigzag stops only at a number the rule gives back unchanged.
Multiply through and phi squared equals phi plus one, whose positive root is one plus root five, over two: the golden ratio.
Fibonacci posed the sequence in 1202 as a puzzle about breeding rabbits; the golden ratio hiding in it was noticed only centuries later.

sens, spec = 0.9, 0.95

card.title: What a positive test is worth

commands.speak: How likely is a positive screening test to be right? Take a test that catches ninety percent of the sick and clears ninety-five percent of the healthy.
A small function: true positives, the sick it catches, against false positives, the healthy it wrongly flags.
Three groups to screen: one person in a thousand ill, one in a hundred, and one in ten.
For each, the chance after one positive, and after a second positive on another test.
The second test starts from the first answer: the people it sees have already tested positive once.
The rows go in as a list of lists, because MicroPython's dictionaries do not keep their order, and the columns would shuffle.
One in a thousand ill: a positive is right less than two percent of the time. One in ten: two times in three.
Picture a thousand people at one in a thousand: one is sick and caught, while five percent of the other 999, about fifty, get false alarms.
A second positive lifts the first row from 1.8 to 24.5 percent: the first test did the work of picking a high-risk group.
The test is the same in every row; only who was tested changed. Prevalence decides what a positive is worth.

commands.speak: When does a leaderboard start telling you who is good? A simulated tournament: twenty players, sixteen rounds, eight places on the board.
A seeded script gives each player a hidden scoring range once, then adds random points from that range every round.
Round one: Mira leads on eleven, Edda on ten. Twelve of the twenty are already off the board, waiting below it.
Then Jo takes over, and leads from round two to round five.
Jo's hidden range is only middling. A few lucky rounds easily beat a better range early on.
By round twelve the top three are Mira, Tor and Pia, and Jo has sunk to fifth.
At the end Mira and Pia tie on a hundred and nineteen, with Finn and Tor just behind.
Those four are four of the five players with the best range. Over sixteen rounds the luck of single rounds averages out, and skill shows.
Six players never reached the board, so you never saw them: the four weakest, and two middling ones.
Jacob Bernoulli proved why in 1713: as trials pile up, an average settles on its true value. The law of large numbers.
So an early board is mostly noise, a late one mostly skill, and a top eight never shows how far behind the rest are.

quiz.question: Jo leads after round five. What best predicts who finishes on top after sixteen rounds?
quiz.right: The scoring range: over sixteen rounds the lucky and unlucky rounds cancel, and four of the five best-ranged players finished first to fourth.

commands.speak: Why can a bar in a race look as if it shrinks while its value grows? A hundred kroner at four interest rates, for thirty years.
Seven percent, five, three and one. At year zero all four bars are the same length: a hundred each.
The rows stay fixed, because nothing here ever overtakes: seven percent stays on top, one percent at the bottom.
After ten years: a hundred and ninety-seven at seven percent, a hundred and ten at one.
The one-percent bar has gained ten kroner, yet it is now only a little over half its old length.
The axis did that. Its end follows the leader, so every tick slides left as the seven-percent bar grows.
On to year thirty: seven hundred and sixty-one against a hundred and thirty-five.
The one-percent bar now fills less than a fifth of the plot, though it has grown by a third.
So on this chart a length says how far behind the leader you are, not how much you have. Read the numbers for that.
The bar chart itself is old: William Playfair drew the first ones in his atlas of trade, in 1786.

quiz.question: Between year ten and year twenty the one-percent bar gets shorter. Did its value fall?

commands.speak: How should a race show a product that hasn't launched yet, or has been shut down? Six simulated products over sixteen years.
A short script grows each one along an S-curve towards its own ceiling. In year one only Aurora and Basalt exist.
Basalt leads on fourteen thousand users, Aurora on eight. For the other four the script writes null: absent, so no row at all.
Zero instead would put four names beside empty bars: products that don't exist, ranked as if they did.
Year four: Cinder launches straight in at eighteen thousand, its real first number, not growing out of a zero it never had.
Year nine: Cinder edges past Basalt, ninety-eight to ninety-seven, and Ember appears at the bottom with six thousand.
Year twelve: Frost launches, a sixth product on a board of five, so for the first time someone waits below the line.
Year fourteen: Basalt is shut down. It does not sink to zero; its row simply leaves, and the others close up.
By year sixteen Cinder leads on a hundred and twenty-seven thousand.
Aurora has sat at fifty-seven thousand since year twelve. A flat bar and a missing bar say different things: stalled, and gone.
Zero is a measurement; null is the absence of one. Tony Hoare, who put null references into a language in 1965, later called them his billion-dollar mistake.

quiz.question: A product launches in year six with 16,000 users. What should the data say for years one to five?
quiz.right: Null: the product did not exist, so there is nothing to measure. A zero would claim it existed with no users, and its bar would grow out of nothing.

commands.speak: A rolling window keeps a line chart on the last twelve months. This race shows what that costs: four regions, one virus, simulated month by month.
Month one: every region starts with one person in a thousand infected. They differ only in how fast the virus spreads.
By month eight Nord, the fastest, peaks with half its people infected at once.
Month twelve. Nord has collapsed, Vest peaked at thirty-three percent in month ten, and the window is full: every month so far is still in view.
From here the axis slides. Each new month that enters on the right pushes the oldest one off the left.
Month eighteen: the view now starts at month six, and Sor, the slowest, reaches its peak, eleven percent.
Month twenty-two. The view starts at month ten, and Nord's fifty percent, the tallest peak of the whole epidemic, has scrolled off the left.
Its line runs on along the bottom, unnamed: this chart gives a name only to the three highest lines, so it forgets the fallen too.
Seen through this window, Sor at seven percent looks like the worst-hit region. It had the mildest wave of the four.
One clue survives: the scale was fixed for the whole race, so it still climbs to sixty, room for a peak no longer shown.
A stock's fifty-two-week high strikes the same bargain: a record that quietly forgets anything older than a year.

quiz.question: At month 22 you see only this window. Which region had the highest peak?
choices: Nord, though its peak is off the chart
quiz.right: Nord: its fifty percent peak in month eight has scrolled out of the window. Sor is highest now only because its wave came last.

commands.speak: Why do five identical urns end up so unequal? Each starts with five balls, and each new ball joins an urn in proportion to what it already holds.
Sixty-five balls in, the shares already differ: Urn C holds twenty-nine percent, Urn B under fourteen.
Nothing sets the urns apart but luck: an urn that wins an early ball becomes likelier to win the next.
By a hundred and eighty-five balls, Urn E leads on thirty percent, and Urn B has fallen under eight.
By four hundred and twenty-five, the fan has stopped opening: E on thirty-two, B on six and a half.
Why it freezes: with twenty-five balls, one more moves an urn's share by three points. With eight hundred, by less than a tenth of a point.
Eight hundred and twenty-five balls. E holds about a third, B about a sixteenth, and E has led at every count since ball one-eighty-five.
Choose the urns evenly instead, and every share would settle near twenty percent. The inequality comes from the rule, not from the urns.
Rerun it with another seed and a different urn wins. George Pólya studied this urn in 1923: each share settles, but where it settles is chance.
So Urn B was never worse at anything. It lost a few early draws, and under this rule the early draws are the ones that count.

quiz.right: Any of the five: the urns are identical, so the winner is whichever got lucky early; late balls barely move the shares.

def corr(n):

    b = 0.8 * a + rng.normal(0, 0.6, n)
    c = 0.5 * b + rng.normal(0, 0.9, n)

commands.speak: Why does a correlation need a big sample? Four measurements from a seeded script, so we know the true correlations exactly.
A with B is truly 0.8, B with C 0.49, A with C 0.39. The fourth variable is pure noise, correlated with nothing.
This is what twenty draws say. B against C reads 0.77, half again the truth, and the noise column is already warm.
Every cell is an estimate, and at twenty people the estimates are poor.
Fifty draws. B against C falls to 0.54, but the noise column still finds correlations near 0.2 where there are none.
Two hundred draws: 0.44, and the noise has cooled to almost nothing.
A thousand, and the matrix settles onto the truth: 0.79, 0.5, 0.39, and a noise column that has faded out.
For pure noise, a sample correlation wanders by about one over the square root of n: 0.22 at twenty people, 0.03 at a thousand.
So a pale-warm 0.2 from twenty people is exactly what noise produces. From a thousand, it would be a real signal.
Ronald Fisher worked out in 1915 how sample correlations scatter around the truth, which is how we know how many people a study needs.

quiz.question: Two unrelated measures, 100 people. About how far will their sample correlation typically stray from zero?
quiz.right: About 0.1: one over the square root of a hundred. A correlation of 0.1 from a hundred people is no evidence of anything.

commands.speak: Did Norway's health spending really double in twelve years? Statistics Norway's health accounts split it four ways.
2007: a hundred and eighty-nine billion kroner. Curative care, the hospitals and doctors, is half of it.
2011 and 2015: the stack keeps climbing.
2019: three hundred and seventy-five billion. Nearly double, in twelve years.
A stack also shows shares. Long-term care grew from about a quarter to thirty percent; medicines shrank from thirteen percent to ten.
But these are current kroner, and a krone in 2019 bought less care than one in 2007.
Here is the same spending in 2015 prices, with the rise in the price of care taken out.
2015 does not move: it is the year whose prices everything is now measured in.
2007 grows to two hundred and sixty-eight billion, and 2019 shrinks to three hundred and thirty-two. A quarter more, not double.
Care got dearer much faster than prices in general. It is mostly wages, and nursing cannot be sped up like a factory: Baumol's cost disease.
And there were fourteen percent more Norwegians to care for. Per person, real spending rose about nine percent.
Money over time needs two corrections before it means much: take out prices, then divide by people.

quiz.question: Health spending in current kroner doubles in twelve years. What does that tell you about care per person?
choices: Nothing yet: prices and population first
quiz.right: Nothing yet: in Norway prices took most of the doubling and population growth took more, leaving about nine percent more real care per person.

request: Did life expectancy in Norway fall during the pandemic? A slope chart of 2019 against 2021

Newborns first. In 2019 a boy could expect to reach eighty-one point two, a girl eighty-four point seven.
People already eighty could expect to reach older ages still: eighty-eight point seven for men, ninety point two for women.
Older than a newborn's figure, because reaching eighty has already ruled out every earlier death.
Three lines rise. Boys gained most: four tenths of a year, about five months.
Only women already eighty lost ground: seven hundredths of a year, under a month.
Neither column is a forecast. Each applies one year's death rates, age by age, to an imagined life: 2021's figure is 2021's mortality, nothing more.
And a slope chart draws a straight line between two years, hiding the one in between: in 2020 women's figure rose to eighty-four point nine.
The chosen years also write the story. Put 2022 in the right column and all four lines fall: boys to eighty point nine.
Norway's pandemic dip came late, in 2022, the year restrictions ended and omicron spread widely.

quiz.question: A slope chart shows a line rising from 2019 to 2021. What do you know about 2020?
choices: Nothing: the chart does not show it
It was the lowest of the three
quiz.right: Nothing: the connector is straight whatever happened between. Norwegian women's figure for 2020 lay above both ends.

Percent changes don't add, they multiply: one and a half, times a half, times four thirds, is exactly one.
The Dow Jones fell about 89 percent from 1929 to 1932. To get back it had to grow ninefold, which took until 1954.
So judge growth by where it starts and ends, never by the average of the percent changes in between.

Same money, same markets. After fifty years: one thousand seven hundred and eighty-two.

This is why John Bogle started the first index fund for ordinary savers in 1976: to keep fees close to nothing.

quiz.question: A fund charges 1 % a year. Over 50 years at 7 %, about how much of the final pot does the fee take?
quiz.right: About forty percent: every dollar the fee takes stops compounding, so the loss grows with the savings.

request: Does a fair coin even out? Flip it five hundred times in light Python and plot the share of heads, then heads minus tails — the plots above the code, typed line by line
title: The share settles, the gap doesn't

elements.code:
import random
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
random.seed(7)
heads, share, gap = 0, [], []
for i in range(1, 501):
    heads += 1 if random.random() < 0.5 else 0
    share.append(heads / i)
    gap.append(heads - (i - heads))

print("heads - tails:", gap[9], "->", gap[-1])

_ = plt.plot([0.5] * 500)
plt.show()
_ = plt.plot(gap)
_ = plt.plot([0] * 500)
plt.show()

commands.speak: Does a fair coin even out: after a run of heads, do the tails catch up? Five hundred flips in light Python, typed as we go.
Seeded, so the same flips come back every time, and three tallies: heads so far, the share of heads, and the gap.
Five hundred flips, each adding a head or nothing.
After every flip, store the share of heads, and heads minus tails.
Print both after ten flips and after all five hundred.
The first plot: the share, with a flat line at one half.
The second: heads minus tails, with a line at zero.
Run it. The share of heads is seventy percent after ten flips, fifty-two after five hundred.
Plotted, the share swings wildly over the first flips, then settles close to a half: the law of large numbers.
But heads minus tails does not shrink. Heads led by four after ten flips, and by twenty after five hundred.
The coin has no memory: after a run of heads, the next flip is still fifty-fifty, so nothing pulls the count back.
The share settles anyway, because a gap of twenty is large among twenty flips and tiny among five hundred: it is swamped, not repaid.
Believing the tails are due is the gambler's fallacy; at Monte Carlo in 1913, black came up twenty-six times in a row while players bet on red.
Change the seed and run it yourself: the share always settles, the gap goes wherever it likes.

quiz.question: A fair coin has come up heads 10 times more than tails. What do you expect after 1,000 more flips?
choices: Still about 10 ahead, give or take
quiz.right: Still about ten ahead, give or take: new flips are fifty-fifty, so they add no correction, only more wandering; the share of heads still nears a half.
