Men høyden skal også dobles, og den doblingen dobler arealet en gang til: 16 kvadratmeter.
Fire ganger så stort, ikke to. Hvorfor?
Det store kvadratet rommer fire kopier av det gamle, to i hver retning.
Areal har to retninger, og hver av dem ble doblet: to ganger to er fire.
Et volum har tre. Dobler du alle mål på en kube, blir volumet to ganger to ganger to: åtte ganger så stort.
Galilei brukte dette i 1638: et dyr dobbelt så høyt veier åtte ganger mer, men beina blir bare fire ganger tykkere. Derfor har elefanter så tykke bein.

quiz.question: En pizza på 40 cm mot en på 20 cm. Hvor mye mer pizza får du?
quiz.right: Fire ganger så mye: diameteren dobles, og en flat pizza vokser i to retninger, to ganger to.

request: Hvorfor er en ytre vinkel lik summen av de to motstående indre?

commands.speak: Hvorfor er en ytre vinkel i en trekant lik summen av de to motstående indre? Ta trekanten A B C.
Vinkelen ved A er 45 grader.
Vinkelen ved C er 75 grader.
Forleng siden A B forbi B. Vinkelen mellom forlengelsen og siden B C er den ytre vinkelen ved B: 120 grader.
Påstanden er at den alltid er summen av de to langt borte, 45 pluss 75. Hvorfor skulle de bestemme den?
Den indre vinkelen ved B er 60 grader. Den og den ytre ligger langs samme rette linje, så de utgjør 180 sammen.
Men de tre vinklene i trekanten utgjør også 180.
Og B pluss den ytre, y, er 180.
B må fylle det samme hullet opp til 180 i begge. Det som er igjen, må være likt: y er A pluss C.
Det finnes også et bilde. Trekk en linje gjennom B, parallell med A C.
Vinkelen ved A glir langs grunnlinja til B. Den parallelle linja skjærer grunnlinja i den samme vinkelen.
Vinkelen ved C, snudd en halv omdreining, passer mellom parallellen og B C: en Z-vinkel mellom to parallelle linjer.
Sammen fyller de nøyaktig den ytre vinkelen: 45 pluss 75 er 120.
Euklid beviste akkurat dette i Elementene, bok én, setning 32, og fikk vinkelsummen på 180 grader med på kjøpet.

quiz.question: En trekant har 30° ved A og 50° ved C. Hva er den ytre vinkelen ved B?
quiz.right: 80 grader: den ytre vinkelen er summen av de to motstående, 30 pluss 50.
quiz.wrong: 100 grader er den indre vinkelen ved B. Den ytre ligger på den andre siden av linja.

request: Hva er en ellipse?

commands.speak: En ellipse ser ut som en klemt sirkel, men hva er den egentlig? Start med to knappenåler, 400 fra hverandre.
Knyt en tråd på 500 mellom dem, og hold den stram med en blyant: 250 til hver nål.
Før blyanten rundt med tråden stram. Den ene biten vokser, og den andre krymper like mye.
Ved enden er bitene 450 og 50. Summen er fortsatt 500, for tråden er den samme.
Sporet blyanten følger, er ellipsen: alle punkter der de to avstandene til nålene har samme sum.
Nålene heter brennpunkter og ligger på den lange aksen. Den er nøyaktig like lang som tråden: ved enden ligger begge bitene langs den.
Skyv nålene sammen, og ellipsen runder seg til en sirkel. En sirkel er en ellipse der de to brennpunktene faller sammen.
Jo lenger fra hverandre nålene står, jo flatere blir ellipsen.
Kepler viste i 1609 at Mars går i en ellipse rundt sola, med sola i det ene brennpunktet, ikke i midten.

quiz.question: Tråden er 500. Et punkt på ellipsen ligger 100 fra det ene brennpunktet. Hvor langt er det til det andre?
quiz.right: 400: avstandene til de to brennpunktene er alltid til sammen trådens lengde, 500.

request: Hva er delene i en symaskin, og hva gjør de?
title: Symaskinen: to tråder, én knute

commands.speak: En symaskin syr flere sting i sekundet, og nesten hele jobben skjer i de to centimeterne rundt nåla.
Overtråden løper ned gjennom armen og gjennom øyet på nåla.
Under bordplata ligger spolen med sin egen tråd, som aldri kommer opp.
Håndhjulet driver begge deler: én omdreining er ett sting.
Nåla stikker ned gjennom stoffet, og idet den løfter seg igjen, blir overtråden hengende som en liten løkke under.
En griper som svinger rundt spolen fanger løkka og fører den hele veien rundt undertråden.
Så strammes tråden, og stinget er ferdig: en knute mellom to tråder. Nåla har aldri vært på den andre siden av stoffet.

request: How does a lock and key open a door?
title: The shear line

spec.title: A pin tumbler lock, in section

commands.speak: A lock is not clever: it is a row of little rods that have to get out of the way of one line.
The plug can only turn if nothing crosses the gap between it and the housing — the shear line.
Right now every steel driver pin straddles that line, pinning the plug to the housing.
The key is not a code to be read. It is a row of heights.
It slides in, tip first, and each cut comes to rest under one brass pin.
The tall cut lifts the short pin far, the shallow cut lifts the long pin a little.
Every joint between brass and steel arrives at the same line at the same moment.
Now nothing bridges the gap, and the plug turns. A wrong key is not rejected — it simply leaves one pin sticking across the line.

request: Hvorfor blir bremselengden fire ganger så lang når farten dobles? Vis formelen.
title: Bremselengden vokser med kvadratet

commands.speak: To biler bremser like hardt på tørr asfalt — den ene i femti, den andre i hundre.
Gjetter man, tenker man gjerne at dobbel fart gir dobbel bremselengde: en rett linje.
Men bremselengden følger denne kurven, som bøyer oppover.
Den rette gjetningen er feil, og formelen sier hvorfor.
Farten står i annen: hele bevegelsesenergien skal bort, og den vokser med kvadratet av farten.
I femti står bilen etter femten meter.
I hundre trengs nesten seksti — fire ganger så langt, ikke dobbelt.
Der den første bilen har stanset, holder den andre fortsatt åttisju kilometer i timen. Dobbel fart er ikke dobbelt så farlig — den er en helt annen kollisjon.

request: What does E = mc² actually say? Show me the curve it comes from.
title: The energy of standing still

elements.x_label: Speed, as a fraction of light speed

commands.speak: Push an object faster and faster, and plot the energy it carries.
This is the real curve: the energy climbs gently, then runs away towards infinity as the speed nears light speed.
That whole curve is one formula — the mass, times light speed squared, divided by that shrinking square root.
Now stand the object still. The square root becomes one, and the famous equation is simply where this curve meets the axis.
So E = mc² is not about explosions or speed — it is the energy a thing has for doing nothing at all.
Newton's old formula tracks it closely up to about half light speed, then falls hopelessly behind.
And because the curve has no top, no amount of pushing ever gets a thing with mass up to light speed.

request: Hvorfor er nordlyset grønt?
title: Fargen forteller høyden

commands.speak: Nordlyset er nesten alltid grønt, og fargen er ikke tilfeldig: den forteller nøyaktig hvor høyt oppe lyset lages.
Slik ser det ut fra bakken — et grønt teppe, ofte med en svak rød rand øverst.
Partikler fra sola treffer atmosfæren ovenfra og slår elektroner løs fra luftas atomer.
Mellom hundre og to hundre og femti kilometer er det oksygenatomer som sender lyset ut, og de lyser grønt.
De samme atomene kan også lyse rødt, men det tar nesten to minutter — og bare der oppe er lufta tynn nok til at atomet får være i fred så lenge.
Under hundre kilometer er lufta så tett at oksygenatomene blir forstyrret før de rekker å lyse; da er det nitrogen som gir fargen, i blått og fiolett.
Så fargen er en høydemåler: grønt betyr oksygen mellom hundre og to hundre og femti kilometer, rødt betyr enda tynnere luft over det, og blått betyr at partiklene har trengt uvanlig dypt ned.

request: Why is the Eiffel Tower shaped like that?
title: The wind curve

commands.speak: The Eiffel Tower's flare looks like decoration. It is arithmetic.
Three hundred metres of open iron — and the force it is really built against is not its own weight but the wind.
Wind pushes on every level, and the higher the level, the longer the lever it has for tipping the whole thing over.
Eiffel's rule was that at every height the legs lean at exactly the angle that turns the push from above into a straight squeeze down the iron.
So the curve is steepest near the ground, where a whole tower's worth of wind has to be carried, and almost straight at the top, where there is nothing above to catch it.
The shape was not drawn, it was solved — and the answer is so sparing that melted down, the entire tower would fill its own square base to a depth of about six centimetres.

request: Hvordan ser Stortinget ut, og hvorfor er det bygget slik?
title: Fasaden er salen sett utenfra

commands.speak: Stortingsbygningen har en rund utbuling midt i fasaden — og den utbulingen forklarer hele huset.
To symmetriske fløyer i gul teglstein strekker seg ut mot hver side.
Og midtpartiet skyter fram mot gata, rundt som et halvt tårn, med tre høye vinduer.
Tegningene er av svensken Emil Victor Langlet, som vant arkitektkonkurransen; huset stod ferdig i 1866.
Men hvorfor er nettopp midten rund?
Buen er ikke pynt — den er en vegg som presses utover fra innsiden.
For sett rett ovenfra er stortingssalen en halvsirkel: et amfi.
Benkeradene bøyer seg rundt ett felles midtpunkt.
I det punktet, ved den rette veggen, står presidenten og talerstolen.
Representantene sitter ikke partivis, men fylkesvis — hvert valgdistrikt samlet i sin kile av salen.
Og denne buede ytterveggen er den samme buen du ser ute i fasaden.
Amfiet gjør at alle vender innover mot hverandre — ikke i to fronter mot hverandre, slik benkene står i det britiske Underhuset.
Så huset er formet av rommet: den runde fasaden er rett og slett stortingssalen sett fra utsiden.

request: Hvorfor blir renters rente så stor? Vis formelen ved kurven.
title: Årene står i eksponenten

commands.speak: Ti tusen kroner til sju prosent i året — og to måter å regne renten på som ender svært ulikt.
Får du bare rente av startbeløpet, kommer det 700 kroner inn hvert år, og beløpet vokser i rett linje.
Men lar du rentene stå på kontoen, gir de selv rente, og kurven bøyer oppover.
Formelen ved kurven: startbeløpet ganget med 1,07 én gang for hvert år som går.
Etter ti år er avstanden nesten ikke til å se — knapt 2 700 kroner skiller dem.
Her har pengene nesten doblet seg, helt som regelen om 72 sier: 72 delt på sju blir omtrent ti år.
Etter tretti år står det 31 000 på den ene kontoen og 76 000 på den andre.
Renten ble aldri satt opp — kurven bare fortsatte å akselerere, fordi sju prosent hele tiden regnes av et større beløp.
Alt ligger i at antall år står som eksponent, og ikke som en faktor du ganger renten med.
Renters rente er derfor ikke en litt bedre rente, men en helt annen kurveform — og den betaler seg først i de siste årene.

request: Hvorfor har en bikube sekskanter? Vis et ekte bilde og skissen.
title: Vegg er voks

elements.credit: Merdal at Turkish Wikipedia · CC BY-SA 3.0

commands.speak: Voks er det dyreste bien lager — hun må spise mange ganger så mye honning for å svette ut ett gram.
Så hver vegg hun sparer, er honning hun beholder — og alle cellene i kaka er sekskanter.
Tre celleformer med nøyaktig samme areal — like mye plass til honning i hver.
Men veggen rundt dem er ikke like lang.
Sekskanten gjerder inn samme areal med kortest vegg av de tre — og vegg er voks.
Bare disse tre formene fyller en flate uten hull igjen — sirkler ville latt luft stå igjen mellom cellene.
Så hun bygger celle etter celle av samme form.
Presset sammen deler naboene vegg, så hver vegg bygges bare én gang.
Mønsteret i fotografiet er nøyaktig denne skissen.
At ingen annen oppdeling i det hele tatt slår sekskantene — heller ikke en med buede vegger — ble først bevist av Thomas Hales i 1999.
Sekskanten er altså ikke pynt: den er den billigste måten å dele opp en flate på.

request: Hvorfor ligger de gamle fabrikkene ved elva?
title: Kraften kunne ikke flytte seg

commands.speak: Ei elv renner ned fra fjellet, og på veien faller den — meter etter meter.
Der fallet er brattest, setter noen et hjul i vannet. Fallet gjør arbeidet: hjulet går rundt så lenge elva renner.
Fabrikken bygges inntil hjulet. Ikke av romantikk: kraften kom ut som en roterende aksel, og en aksel rekker noen få meter.
Arbeiderne må bo der maskinene står, så boligene kommer etter. Slik vokser en hel by rundt ett fall i ei elv.
Så kom strømmen. Nå kunne kraften gå i en ledning — like gjerne ti mil som ti meter.
Fra da av kunne fabrikken ligge hvor som helst: ved jernbanen, ved havna, ved arbeidsfolket.
De gamle fabrikkene står der ennå, ved fossen. De ble bygget den gangen kraften ikke kunne flytte seg — så fabrikken måtte flytte til kraften.

request: Why does a vaccine protect people who never got it?
title: The road, not the blood

commands.speak: Five neighbours on one street. The last one is three weeks old — too young for any vaccine that exists.
A virus turns up at the first door. It has no wings and no legs: the only way it moves is from one person to the next.
Left alone it walks the street door by door, and on the fourth step it reaches the baby.
Now give two of them the vaccine — the second and the third, nobody else.
The virus still reaches the second door. And there it stops: in this simple picture the vaccinated neighbour does not pass it on, so the road simply ends.
The baby is as unvaccinated as before, and just as susceptible. Nothing changed inside it. What changed was the road.
That is herd immunity: a vaccine protects the person who takes it, and the gap that person leaves protects everyone standing behind them.

request: Why does a higher frequency squeeze the wave?

commands.speak: A sound has a pitch. What does a higher pitch look like on the wave?
Here is a wave that repeats once per unit of time: frequency one.
Mark one point on it, so we can watch it.
Raise the frequency and the same stretch of time holds more and more cycles: the wave is squeezed, and the point rides up and down four times as often.
Four cycles per unit of time: that is what a higher pitch is.
As the point slides along the squeezed wave, you feel how fast it now has to move.

request: What is the tangent at a point, and how does it turn as the point slides?

spec.title: The tangent turns with the point

elements.text: The tangent turns with the point

commands.speak: A curve bends. How steep is it at one point?
Take the sine curve.
Pick a point on it.
The tangent is the straight line that touches the curve there and leans exactly as the curve leans: its slope is the derivative, cosine of x.
As the point slides along, the tangent turns with it: flat at the crest, steepest where the curve crosses zero, flat again in the trough.
That turning line is the derivative made visible.

request: Does the equilibrium follow when demand shifts?

commands.speak: Incomes rise and people want more of everything. Where does the market settle now?
Demand slopes down: the higher the price, the less is bought.
Supply slopes up: the higher the price, the more is offered.
Where they cross, the market clears. This point is defined by the two curves.
The wedge between them, up to the crossing, is the gain the market creates.
Keep a faint copy of where demand stands today.

Now demand shifts right. The crossing point and its guide lines slide up the supply curve, and the wedge grows to the new crossing. Nothing is redrawn by hand, because they were defined by the curves.
Higher price, higher quantity: the new equilibrium.
The old demand curve can go.

request: What happens to the angle when one arm turns?

spec.title: An angle is made of its arms

elements.text: An angle is made of its arms

commands.speak: What is an angle, really?
Two arms from one vertex. This one stays.
This one we will turn.
The angle is the opening between them, and it writes its own size.
Turn the arm about the vertex and the arc widens with it, the number climbing as it goes: the angle is nothing but the two arms.
Turn it back past the first arm and the opening shrinks to nothing, then grows the other way round.
Move an arm, and the angle follows. It was defined by them.

request: How do you solve 2x + 3 = 11?

commands.speak: How do you solve 2x + 3 = 11 for x?
Two things stand between x and being alone: a plus three, and a coefficient of two.
Keep the top line as it was, and work the next step on a copy.
Subtract three from both sides: the 3 leaves, and 11 drops to 8.
Copy again, and finish it on this new line.
Divide both sides by two: 2x becomes x, 8 becomes 4.
x equals 4 — and unlike scratch work, every earlier line is still there to check.

request: What does the ICER compare?

commands.speak: What does the ICER — the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio — actually compare?
C one minus C zero, in red, is the extra cost of the new treatment; E one minus E zero, in blue, is the extra effect it buys.
Call those differences delta C and delta E: the ratio is just cost per unit of extra benefit.
Five hundred dollars more, for one tenth of a year of extra life, is five thousand dollars for every year gained.
That is what the ICER always compares: money against health, boiled into one number.

request: Why do cos and sin draw a circle?

spec.title: Why cos and sin draw a circle

elements.text: Why do cos and sin draw a circle?

commands.speak: A point sits one unit from the center. Nudge its angle around — what shape does it trace?
Start it at angle zero: one unit out along x, none up — cos zero is one, sin zero is zero.
Every angle t gives a new point, cos t and sin t — the path it leaves behind grows as the angle does.
Sweep the angle through a full turn and watch the point trace its path, always the same one unit from the center.
The arm's length never changes, only its direction — so the point can only ever land one unit out. That's why cosine and sine draw a circle.

request: Why is a life-year gained in thirty years worth so little today?

commands.speak: Vaccinate a child today and you prevent a broken hip in fifty years. Every health-economic guideline says that future year of good health counts for less than one today.
How much less — and does it change what we ought to be funding? Start with no discounting at all. The weight on a year of health is flat at one: a year is a year, whenever it happens to arrive.
The rule that bends that line is a single expression — a year t years away counts one over one plus r, raised to the power t.
Right now the rate r is zero, so the power does nothing and every year still weighs a full one.
Turn r up to three and a half percent — the rate most guidelines actually use — and the line sags away from one. Nothing else in the picture was redrawn: the curve is the formula.
Read off year thirty, the year that hip fracture would have happened.
Put thirty into the same expression and it says it plainly: that year of health counts as about a third of a year lived today.
Notice what that is not. It is not a small correction — nearly two thirds of the value has quietly gone.
Now add up everything a treatment ever delivers, not just one year. Shade the first twenty years of benefit.
And shade what comes after: year twenty to year sixty, plus a thin tail that runs off the edge of this chart and never quite stops.
Those two areas are the same size. At three and a half percent, half of everything a treatment could ever deliver — from here to eternity — lands in its first twenty years.

So discounting is not a footnote in the appendix. It is the reason prevention that pays off in fifty years has to fight for money against treatment that pays off tomorrow — and why the choice of r is argued over as hard as the clinical evidence.

request: Do people live longer if the cancer is found earlier?

commands.speak: Screening finds cancers earlier, and patients in screened groups have far better five-year survival. That looks like proof the screening works.
Follow one patient along this line of years and see whether it is. The tumour begins here, in year two, quietly — years before anyone could feel a thing.
In year eight it grows enough to cause symptoms, and that is when the diagnosis gets written down.
In year eleven the patient dies of it.

Survival is measured from the diagnosis to the death: three years. That is the number that goes into the statistics — and the ruler is drawn from the figure itself, so it can only ever say what the picture says.
Now live the same life a second time, in a country that runs a screening programme. Same tumour, starting the same year — and, keep your eye on this, the same day of death.
One line joins the two deaths. Nothing that happens to the left of it is going to move it.
To begin with, the second patient is also found in year eight, by symptoms, and the second ruler reads the same three years.
Now switch the screening on. The scan picks the tumour up in year four, four years before it would have spoken up. That is the one and only thing that changes in this picture.
And measured survival has more than doubled: seven years instead of three. Nobody was cured. The ruler simply starts further left.

Look at the five-year mark and it gets worse. The first patient is dead within five years of diagnosis; the second is comfortably alive at five. Five-year survival goes from zero to a hundred percent without a single day of life being added.

This is lead-time bias, and it is why a screening programme can never be judged on survival. The one question the flattered ruler cannot answer is the only one that matters: does that death line move to the right?

request: How can a calculator work out sin(1.2) with nothing but plus and times?

spec.title: A polynomial learns the sine curve

elements.text: A polynomial learns the sine curve

commands.speak: Your calculator has no idea what sine means. Its hardware can add, multiply and divide, and that is the whole list. Ask it for the sine of 1.2 and it answers in microseconds anyway.
What is it actually computing? This is the shape it has to produce out of arithmetic alone.
And this is where it starts: the polynomial P of x equals x. A straight line, which is about as far from a wave as you can get.
Except right here. Near zero the line and the curve are indistinguishable — the sine of a hundredth really is a hundredth, out to six decimal places.
So add one correction: minus x cubed over six.
Watch what that buys. The line bends over and now follows the curve out past the first crest — and beyond that it dives away, further off than the straight line ever was.
Add the next term, plus x to the fifth over a hundred and twenty.
The agreement pushes outward — and so does the place where it gives up.
One more term.
Now four terms of pure arithmetic hold the curve through an entire hump before they let go.

Here is the part that should feel strange. Those denominators — six, a hundred and twenty, five thousand and forty — are the factorials that come out of differentiating sine at this one point. Nothing in the recipe ever looked at what sine does out at x equals three.

The polynomial was told about a single point and it reproduces a whole stretch of the curve. That is what a Taylor series spends: local information, bought at one place, to buy the neighbourhood around it.

And notice what you never get for free. The fit spreads outward from that point; it never improves everywhere at once. Far enough out, the polynomial always loses — and the more terms you add, the more violently it runs away when it finally does.

request: How could anyone see whether two tones were in tune, a century before electronic tuners?

spec.title: Reading an interval off a picture

elements.text: Reading an interval off a picture

commands.speak: A tuning fork with a small mirror glued to it, a beam of light, and a second fork turned at right angles. That was Jules Lissajous's apparatus in 1855, and an oscilloscope did the same job a century later.

Two tones go in and a picture comes out; the whole question is what the picture tells you. One tone pushes the spot of light left and right. The other pushes it up and down. On its own, either one would just draw a line.
Sound both at once, at the same pitch, and the spot has to obey both at the same time.
It traces a circle. Two tones in perfect unison, a quarter of a cycle apart in phase, and the beam goes round and round the same closed loop forever.
Now raise the second fork by an octave — exactly twice the frequency of the first.

A figure of eight — and it is not decoration, it is a reading. Count where the curve kisses the edge of the box: twice along the top for every once on the right-hand side. Two to one. The picture has counted the ratio for you.

A perfect fifth is three to two, so try that. This one needs the sideways sweep to run twice over before the pattern closes on itself, which is the two in three-to-two showing up as time rather than shape.

Three touches along the top for every two on the side. You can read the interval straight off the glass without knowing a single frequency in hertz — only their ratio, which is all an interval ever was.

And here is the part that turned a curiosity into a tuning instrument. Detune that fifth by a whisper — a tenth of a hertz — and the ratio is no longer exactly three to two. A frequency that is slightly wrong is the same thing as a phase that keeps creeping, so the closed figure stops standing still and begins to roll over.
The speed of that rolling is the size of your error. It is the same drift you hear as beats when two notes are nearly together — the wobble that gets slower and slower as you close in.

So nobody read a number off this apparatus. You turned the peg until the picture stopped moving. A figure that holds perfectly still is an exact ratio — and that is a far finer test of tuning than any ear or any dial of the period could manage.

request: Can a treatment be better for mild cases, better for severe cases, and still lose overall?

spec.title: Better in each group, worse overall

elements.text: Better in each group, worse overall

elements.x_label: % of this treatment's patients whose case was severe

commands.speak: A hospital compares two treatments for kidney stones. Treatment A does better on the small stones. Treatment A also does better on the large stones. And when every patient is pooled into one table, treatment B comes out ahead.

All three statements are read off the same data, all three are true, and these numbers are close to a real published comparison. Here is treatment A's recovery rate, plotted against how severe the cases were: 93 percent when the stones are small, sliding down to 73 percent on the worst ones.
And treatment B, the same way: 87 down to 69. B's line sits below A's the whole way across. There is no kind of patient for whom B is the better bet.
So on the mild cases the comparison is 93 against 87. A wins.
Keep that line where it is, and work the severe cases on a copy underneath.
Seventy-three against sixty-nine. A wins again, by four points.
Now pool the patients. A treatment's overall rate is not some new number: it is a dot sitting on its own line, at the average severity of the patients that treatment happened to be given.
Give both treatments the same mix of patients and the dots sit above one another — A's on top, exactly as the two group comparisons promised.

But that is not what happened. The surgeons trusted treatment A, so they gave it the difficult stones and left the easy ones to B. A's dot slides right into the hard cases; B's slides left into the easy ones. Neither line moves — only which part of it each treatment is being judged on.
Add the pooled comparison as a third line.
Seventy-eight against eighty-two and a half. The inequality has turned around, and nobody touched a single patient's outcome.
Look at what the two dots are now. They are not above one another any more, so they are not answering the same question: one is an average of hard cases, the other an average of easy ones.

That is Simpson's paradox, and the useful way to hold on to it is this: a pooled rate is a weighted average, and whoever decided which patients got which treatment decided the weights. The comparison you can trust is the one where the dots stand on the same vertical line.

request: The test is 99% accurate and mine came back positive. Am I probably ill?

spec.title: What a positive test is actually worth

elements.text: What a positive test is actually worth

commands.speak: You take a test for a disease. The test is ninety-nine percent accurate, which is a genuinely good test, and it comes back positive. How worried should you be? This is the question that most people — including, in study after study, most doctors — get badly wrong. Here are a hundred people like you.
In this population one person in a hundred actually has the disease. Just this one. That is what a one percent base rate looks like when you draw it instead of stating it.

The question you want answered is the reverse of the one the test answers. Not how often the test is right, but this: given that the result came back positive, what are the chances the disease is there? Bayes's rule turns one into the other.
Test all hundred people. The test catches ninety-nine percent of real cases, so the one person who is ill duly tests positive. The test has done exactly what it promises.

But being ninety-nine percent accurate also means being wrong about one healthy person in a hundred. There are ninety-nine healthy people in this square, so that is about one more positive result — this person here, who is perfectly well.
Two people in this square get the phone call. Only one of them is ill. And nothing distinguishes them: both were told the same thing by the same reliable test.
Keep the rule and put the numbers on a copy below it.
A half. A coin flip, from a test that is right ninety-nine times out of a hundred. The arithmetic agrees with the square: two positives, one of them real.
Now change one number — and it is not a number about the test.

Screen for something rarer, one case in a thousand, with the very same test on the very same machine, and a positive result now means about nine percent. Nine times out of ten, that letter is a false alarm.

The reason is visible in the square rather than in the algebra. False positives are drawn from the healthy crowd, so their number grows with how big that crowd is. True positives can only ever come out of the tiny sick minority — and rarity shrinks that minority faster than any plausible test can compensate.

So the accuracy printed on the box is not the number you want, and it never was. The same test means one thing for a patient who already has symptoms and something quite different in a mass screening programme — because the thing that changed was not the test, but who you pointed it at.

request: Why is the production possibilities frontier bowed outward and not a straight line?
title: Why the frontier bows

commands.speak: A country can put its people into bread or into steel, and the shape of the line between them is what tells you what a choice actually costs.
The natural guess is a straight line: hand over the same amount of bread for every extra tonne of steel.
It is a sensible guess, and it quietly assumes something that is never true — that one worker is as good as another at both jobs.
People are not interchangeable, so the line is not straight.
It bows outward, and the bulge is the whole story.
Move the first few people into steel and you pick the ones who were worst at baking — barely any bread is lost.
Move the last few and you are taking your best bakers to a job they are bad at. The same tonne of steel now costs a fortune in bread.
So a straight frontier would describe a world where nobody is especially good at anything. The bow IS the fact that people differ.

request: Why can a heat pump deliver more heat than the electricity it uses?
title: Where a heat pump's extra heat comes from

spec.title: Where a heat pump's extra heat comes from

commands.speak: A heat pump takes one unit of electricity and puts three or four units of heat into the house. That sounds like something for nothing, so it is worth following where the extra comes from.
The same refrigerant goes round and round these four parts, and the whole trick is what happens in each one.
Outside in the cold, the refrigerant is colder still — so heat flows into it. Even at minus five, the air has plenty of heat left to give up.
The compressor squeezes that gas, and squeezing a gas makes it hot — hotter than the living room. This is the step the electricity pays for.
Now the refrigerant is the hottest thing in the room, so heat flows the only way heat ever flows: out of it and into the air you breathe.
The valve lets it expand and turn cold again, ready to go back outside and collect another load.
Round it goes, carrying heat inwards every time.

So the electricity never became the heat. It paid for the squeezing — the heat was already outside all along, and the pump only carried it in. A fan heater cannot beat one for one, because it has nothing to carry.

request: Why does a bigger sample make a poll more accurate — and why doesn't the size of the country matter?
title: What a poll's margin really depends on

spec.title: What a poll's margin really depends on

commands.speak: A poll asks a thousand people and then reports a number for five million. Whether you can trust it comes down to one curve.
This is how far off the poll can be, as the number of people asked grows. It drops steeply, then flattens out.
Ask a hundred people and the answer is give or take ten points — useless for anything close.
Ask four times as many and the error halves, to five points.
Four times again, and it only halves once more. Every halving costs four times the interviews, which is exactly why nobody polls a hundred thousand people.
And nothing in that arithmetic ever asked how many people there were to begin with.

quiz.question: A poll of 1,000 Norwegians and a poll of 1,000 Americans. Which has the smaller margin of error?
choices: The Norwegian one — a smaller country to cover
The American one — more people to draw from
quiz.right: The same. The margin depends on how many you asked, not on how many you could have asked.
quiz.wrong: The same. The margin depends on how many you asked, not on how many you could have asked.

commands.speak: A spoonful tells you how the soup tastes whether the pot is small or enormous — as long as you stirred it first. That stirring is the random sample, and it is the part that actually goes wrong.

request: Hvorfor blir ventetiden hos legen så mye lengre når kontoret er nesten fullbooket?
title: Ventetid og slakk

commands.speak: Hvor fullt bør et legekontor bookes? Svaret avgjør hvor lenge du sitter på venterommet, og det ligger ikke der de fleste tror.
Ventetiden vokser ikke jevnt med hvor fullt det er. Den bøyer av oppover, og til slutt nesten rett opp.
Ved åtti prosent booking venter du litt, men dagen henger sammen.
Ved nittifem prosent, bare femten prosentpoeng mer, er ventetiden mangedoblet.
Grunnen er at pasienter ikke kommer jevnt utover dagen. De klumper seg.
Er det luft igjen i dagen, spises en forsinkelse opp av den luften. Er det ikke det, arver neste pasient hele forsinkelsen, og pasienten etter der igjen.
Så ventetid måler ikke hvor hardt de jobber der inne. Den måler hvor lite slakk de har igjen å ta forsinkelser med.

title: An epidemic peaks because it runs out of people to infect
elements:

    type: code
    language: python
    show: left
    width: 900
    pane: controls
    controls: [beta, gamma, days]
    code: |-
      import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
      def sir(beta=(0.1, 1.0, 0.05), gamma=(0.05, 0.5, 0.05), days=(30, 200)):
          s, i, r = 0.99, 0.01, 0.0
          S, I, R = [s], [i], [r]
          for _ in range(days):
              new, rec = beta * s * i, gamma * i
              s, i, r = s - new, i + new - rec, r + rec
              S.append(s); I.append(i); R.append(r)
          plt.plot(S, label="susceptible"); plt.plot(I, label="infected"); plt.plot(R, label="recovered")
          plt.ylim(0, 1); plt.legend(); print("peak infected:", round(max(I), 3))
      sir()

request: What does a sampling distribution look like if I only have one sample? Can I bootstrap it in R?

commands.speak: One sample of waiting times, and three knobs: its size, how many resamples, and a button for a fresh sample.
The sample: forty exponential waiting times, mean about four.
The trick: resample the sample WITH replacement, take the mean, and repeat — the data pretends to be the population.
Print the sample mean and the spread of the resampled means, then draw them.
That histogram is the sampling distribution of the mean, built from one sample. Its width is the standard error — no formula needed.
Slide the sample size up and watch the histogram narrow. Press Resample: a different sample, the same shape.

title: A cohort walks through three states

    language: python
    show: left
    width: 900
    pane: controls
    controls: [p_sick, p_dead, years]

      import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

request: How does Morse code spell letters with just two signals — and can I send SOS?

commands.speak: Morse code spells every letter with just two signals, a short dot and a long dash. So which letter gets which pattern?
Each letter gets its own pattern of one to four signals.
E, the commonest letter in English, is a single dot.
T, the second commonest, is a single dash.
Q, which you rarely need, takes four: dash, dash, dot, dash.
The shortest patterns went to the letters used most, so an ordinary message needs far fewer signals than alphabetical order would give.
The red rows are the word we'll send. S is three dots, and O is three dashes.
To send, use the four pads: dot, dash, gap to end a letter, and send. Or hold the space bar, briefly for a dot.
What you send appears as a strip, with the letters it decodes to above it.
A dash lasts three dots, so the ear tells them apart by length alone.
The gap is a signal too: without it, three dots and three dashes are just six sounds the listener must split somewhere.
SOS stands for nothing. It was adopted in 1906 because three dots, three dashes, three dots is easy to send and hard to mistake.

ask.question: Send SOS on the key.
ask.right: Three short, three long, three short: nine signals, each letter closed with a gap.
ask.wrong: End each letter with the gap pad, then press send.

quiz.question: Why is E a single dot?
quiz.right: It is the commonest letter in English: short codes for frequent letters make every message quicker to send.

request: Why does the Tower of Hanoi take 2^n − 1 moves?

commands.speak: The Tower of Hanoi asks how few moves shift a whole tower to the right peg. The rules: one disk at a time, never a larger on a smaller.
Take three disks. Before the biggest can move anywhere, what has to be true?
Both disks above it must be out of the way, stacked on the middle peg. That is a two-disk tower, moved: three moves.
Then the big disk crosses, in one move.
And the two-disk tower moves again, onto it: three more. Three, one, three: seven.
The same holds for any size: to move n disks, move the tower above the biggest twice, plus one move for the biggest.
That twice is the whole story. Each extra disk doubles the work, and adds one.
One, three, seven, fifteen, thirty-one: always one less than a power of two. A guess of two more per disk would say nine for four disks; it takes fifteen.
Édouard Lucas sold the puzzle in 1883 with a legend of monks moving sixty-four disks. At a move a second, that takes about 585 billion years.
Back to the start. Now it's your tower.

ask.question: Move the tower to the right peg. Can you do it in seven?
ask.right: Solved. Seven is the fewest: the small pair aside in three, the big disk over, the pair back on top in three.
ask.wrong: Get the top two onto the middle peg first; that frees the big disk.

quiz.question: Five disks take 31 moves. How many does six take?
quiz.right: 63: the five-disk tower moves twice, 31 moves each, plus one move for the biggest disk.

request: How an XOR gate works.

commands.speak: XOR means exclusive or: one input or the other, but not both.
Two switches feed the gate.
The bulb lights when the gate's output is one.

ask.question: Find an input that lights the bulb.
ask.right: Exactly one switch on — that is what exclusive means.
ask.wrong: Flip a switch and watch the bulb.

request: A xylophone I can play.

commands.speak: A xylophone is a row of tuned bars: hit one and it rings at its own pitch.
Eight bars, C to C — one octave. The long bars ring low, and every bar to the right is a little shorter and a little higher.
Tap a bar and it sounds and joins the line above, or press its number; done delivers the tune.
The first, third and fifth bars — C, E and G — are a major chord: the three notes a tune usually comes home to.

ask.question: Play C4, E4 and G4, then press done.
ask.right: That is a C major chord, spelled out one bar at a time.
ask.wrong: Bars one, three and five, in that order — then done.

request: Sort the bars like bubble sort.

commands.speak: Bubble sort walks along a row and swaps any two neighbours that are in the wrong order.
Six bars, jumbled, each as tall as the value written on it.
One rule, and it is the whole algorithm: only bars standing next to each other may trade places. A bar can be dragged onto its neighbour, or the two clicked in turn, and the counter keeps the tally.

ask.question: Sort the bars from shortest to tallest.
ask.right: Seven swaps is the fewest this row allows — and notice what happened on the way: the tallest bar bubbled to the end on the very first pass.
ask.wrong: Only neighbours may swap — drag a bar onto the one beside it, or click the two in turn.

request: Why does tic-tac-toe always end in a draw?

commands.speak: Tic-tac-toe between two careful players always ends in a draw. Why can't the first player force a win? Watch one game.
X opens in a corner.
O takes the centre, the square on four of the eight lines.
X takes the opposite corner.
O takes another corner. It looks natural, and it loses.
O now threatens the diagonal, so X must block in the bottom corner. And that one block makes two threats.
Up the left side and along the bottom: a fork. O can block only one of them.
O blocks the bottom row.
X completes the left column and wins.
Every win in this game comes from a fork, because a single threat can always be blocked.
So rewind to O's second move.
This time O plays an edge, and makes a threat of its own, down the middle column.
X must block at the bottom. A player busy blocking never gets the free move a fork needs.
Answer threat with threat, and the board fills up with no winner. Every opening goes that way under perfect play.
In 1952 Sandy Douglas put noughts and crosses on Cambridge's EDSAC computer: one of the first video games.
Your board: you are X. The computer plays win, block, centre, then the first free corner: the rule that just lost.

ask.question: Play a game. Hold at least a draw, or find the fork.
ask.right: Held. Against a perfect defender nobody does better than a draw; against this rule, corner then opposite corner wins.
ask.wrong: O got three in a row. Block its threat before building your own.

quiz.question: X holds two opposite corners, O the centre. Where should O play?
quiz.right: An edge: it makes a threat X must block, so X never gets the free move a fork needs.

request: Why does a disease with a higher R0 need so many more people vaccinated before it stops spreading?

elements.code:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
r0 = Slider(1.2, 8.0, step=0.2, default=2.0, label="R0")
efficacy = Slider(0.5, 1.0, step=0.05, default=0.9, label="Vaccine efficacy")
coverage = Slider(0.0, 1.0, step=0.05, default=0.6, label="Coverage")
r = np.linspace(1.05, 8, 200)
plt.plot(r, 1 - 1 / r, label="share that must be immune")
need = 1 - 1 / r0
plt.scatter([r0], [need], zorder=3)
plt.axhline(coverage * efficacy, color="gray", linestyle="--", label="immune today")
plt.xlabel("R0"); plt.ylabel("share immune"); plt.ylim(0, 1); plt.legend()
print("R0", r0, "needs", round(100 * need), "% immune; today", round(100 * coverage * efficacy), "%")

commands.speak: Measles needs about nineteen in twenty of us protected before it stops; flu manages with far fewer. The whole difference is one number — how many people each case infects, R0 — and it is the first knob.
The other two knobs are what a vaccination programme controls: how well the vaccine works, and how many people take it.

The curve is the share that must be immune, one minus one over R0. The dot is where we stand today: at an R0 of two, half of us must be immune — and with ninety percent efficacy at sixty percent coverage, we are just past it.
Walk R0 from one point six up to nearly six. The share that must be immune leaps from under forty percent to two thirds by three — and then it only crawls: three quarters, then four fifths.
That is the surprise: most of the demand for immunity is bought between R0 of one and three. A disease twice as contagious as another does not need twice the coverage — the threshold flattens.
Now try it yourself: set R0 to fifteen-ish for measles by sliding it to the top, and see how far coverage must rise before the dashed line clears the dot.

request: Hvorfor gir en god test så mange falske alarmer når sykdommen er sjelden?

elements.code:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
forekomst = Slider(0.001, 0.2, step=0.001, default=0.01, label="Forekomst")
sensitivitet = Slider(0.5, 1.0, step=0.01, default=0.9, label="Sensitivitet")
spesifisitet = Slider(0.5, 1.0, step=0.01, default=0.95, label="Spesifisitet")
n = 100000
syke = n * forekomst
ekte = syke * sensitivitet
falske = (n - syke) * (1 - spesifisitet)
ppv = ekte / (ekte + falske)
plt.bar(["ekte syke", "falske alarmer"], [ekte, falske])
plt.ylabel("positive prøver av 100 000")
plt.ylim(0, 10000)
print("Av de positive er", round(100 * ppv), "% faktisk syke")

commands.speak: En test som finner ni av ti syke og frikjenner nitten av tjue friske høres nesten perfekt ut. Likevel kan de fleste som får positivt svar være friske. Det avgjørende er den første knappen: hvor vanlig sykdommen er.
De to andre knappene er testens egne egenskaper: sensitivitet, andelen syke den fanger, og spesifisitet, andelen friske den slipper gjennom.

Av hundre tusen testede er tusen syke. Testen finner ni hundre av dem — men den slår også alarm for fem prosent av de nittini tusen friske, altså nesten fem tusen. Bare femten av hundre positive er faktisk syke.

Gå forekomsten ned fra én av ti til én av tusen. Søylen med ekte syke krymper, søylen med falske alarmer står nesten stille — og andelen ekte syke blant de positive faller fra to av tre til under to av hundre.
Testen ble aldri dårligere. Det er de friske som er så mange at selv fem prosent av dem drukner de syke. Derfor screener man sjeldne sykdommer bare i grupper der de er vanlige.
Prøv selv: skru spesifisiteten helt opp mot hundre prosent og se hvor mye mer det hjelper enn å skru opp sensitiviteten.

request: Why does a trial with forty patients so often miss a real effect that a trial with four hundred finds every time?

spec.title: Statistical power, one sample size at a time

elements.code:
library(ggplot2)
n <- Slider(10, 400, default = 40, label = "Patients per arm")
effect <- Slider(0.1, 1.0, step = 0.05, default = 0.4, label = "Effect size")
sizes <- seq(10, 400, by = 10)
pw <- sapply(sizes, function(k) power.t.test(n = k, delta = effect, sd = 1)$power)
here <- power.t.test(n = n, delta = effect, sd = 1)$power
cat("power at", n, "per arm:", round(100 * here), "%\n")
ggplot(data.frame(n = sizes, power = pw), aes(n, power)) + geom_line() +
  geom_point(data = data.frame(n = n, power = here), size = 3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.8, linetype = "dashed") + ylim(0, 1)

commands.speak: Two trials test the same drug, and the drug genuinely works. The small one reports no significant difference; the large one reports a clear effect. Neither is wrong — the first knob, patients per arm, decides how often a real effect shows up at all.
The second knob is the effect itself, measured in standard deviations — a small effect needs far more patients to surface than a large one.
The curve is statistical power: the chance a trial of that size detects the effect. The dot is our trial, forty per arm. It sits near forty percent — a coin toss, weighted against us.

Walk the arms up from forty to four hundred. Power leaps from a coin toss to ninety-five percent by a hundred and sixty, and is all but certain by two hundred and eighty — the last hundred and twenty patients buy almost nothing.
That is why trials are sized before they start: the cost of patients rises in a straight line, but what they buy flattens out.
Now shrink the effect to a fifth of a standard deviation and watch the whole curve sink — then find how many patients per arm it takes to get back to eighty percent.

request: How does turning beta and gamma change the epidemic curve?

elements.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
beta = Slider(0.1, 1.0, step=0.01, default=0.3, label="beta")
gamma = Slider(0.05, 0.5, step=0.01, default=0.1, label="gamma")
S, I, R = [0.999], [0.001], [0.0]
for k in range(1500):
    new, rec = beta * S[-1] * I[-1] * 0.1, gamma * I[-1] * 0.1
    S.append(S[-1] - new); I.append(I[-1] + new - rec); R.append(R[-1] + rec)
days = [k * 0.1 for k in range(len(S))]
_ = plt.plot(days, S, label="S")
_ = plt.plot(days, I, label="I")
_ = plt.plot(days, R, label="R")
_ = plt.xlim(0, 150); _ = plt.ylim(0, 1); _ = plt.legend()
print("R0", round(beta / gamma, 1), "| peak", round(100 * max(I)), "% on day", round(days[I.index(max(I))]), "| never infected", round(100 * S[-1]), "%")

commands.speak: An epidemic model has two rates, beta and gamma. What does each one control? Everyone starts here, susceptible.
Contact with an infectious person moves you across, at a rate beta times the share who are infectious.
Recovery moves you on at rate gamma, one over the days you stay infectious: gamma 0.1 means about ten days.
Their ratio, beta over gamma, is R nought: how many people one case infects in a population with no immunity.
Now the same model as a running simulation, with both rates as knobs.
Beta at 0.3, gamma at 0.1: R nought is three.
Infections peak at thirty percent of the population, around day thirty-nine, and six percent are never infected.
Now double both rates together: twice the contacts, but each case infectious for half as long.
The same curve, squeezed into half the time: the peak is still thirty percent, now on day nineteen, and still six percent escape.
Doubling both is just running the clock twice as fast. The rates set the speed; only their ratio sets the size.
Now double only beta, keeping ten infectious days. R nought becomes six.
The peak jumps to over half the population, and almost nobody escapes.
Kermack and McKendrick showed in 1927 that the share ever infected depends on R nought alone: at three, about ninety-four percent.
So shortening how long cases stay infectious, by isolation or treatment, raises gamma, and that shrinks an epidemic rather than merely speeding it up.
Try two different pairs with the same ratio, and watch the curve keep its height while it moves in time.

quiz.question: A new variant passes on twice as easily per contact, but people also recover twice as fast. Compared with the old one, its epidemic is…
quiz.right: Just as large, but quicker: beta over gamma, R nought, is unchanged, and R nought alone sets the peak and the final size.

request: Why is the regression slope the covariance divided by the variance?

spec.title: Where the regression slope comes from

elements.text: Why is the slope Cov(x, y) / Var(x)?
how x and y move together, per unit of how x moves alone

commands.speak: Why is the regression slope the covariance of x and y divided by the variance of x?
On top: every deviation of x, in blue, multiplied by the matching deviation of y, in red, and summed. When x and y move together, those products are mostly positive.
Underneath: the squared deviations of x alone. So the slope asks how much x and y move together, per unit of how much x moves by itself.
Divide both sums by n and the names appear: covariance over variance. Same fraction, shorter words.
That is the whole least-squares slope: co-movement, scaled by the spread of the predictor.

request: What do μ and σ do in the normal distribution's formula?

spec.title: μ and σ in the normal density

elements.text: What do μ and σ do in the normal formula?
σ: how wide the bell is

commands.speak: What do mu and sigma actually do inside the normal distribution's formula?
Look at the exponent first. x minus mu, squared: the further x is from mu, in red, the more negative the exponent, and the lower the curve. So mu is simply where the peak sits.
Sigma, in blue, divides that distance. A large sigma makes every distance count for less, so the bell spreads out; a small sigma punishes distance, and the bell narrows.
Name the standardised distance z: how many sigmas x lies from mu. The exponent becomes minus z squared over two, the same bell for every mu and sigma.
Everything else in the formula is just the constant that makes the area under the bell equal to one.

request: Why are future QALYs discounted?

elements.text: r = 3–4 % a year in most guidelines

commands.speak: Why are quality-adjusted life years in the future worth less than the same years now?
Start with the undiscounted sum: each period of length delta t, in violet, weighted by its utility u, in blue, between zero and one.
Discounting divides each year's contribution by one plus r, raised to how far away that year is. A year of good health ten years out counts for less than one today.
Guidelines typically set r around three to four percent a year: not because health matters less later, but because people, and budgets, prefer benefits sooner.
The same discount rate is applied to costs, so the ICER compares like with like.

request: Hvordan henger gjennomsnitt og standardavvik sammen?

elements.text: Hvordan henger gjennomsnitt og standardavvik sammen?

commands.speak: Hvordan henger gjennomsnittet og standardavviket sammen?
Gjennomsnittet, x-strek i rødt, er summen av alle verdiene delt på antallet. Det er midtpunktet dataene fordeler seg rundt.

Standardavviket bruker det samme midtpunktet: hver verdi minus x-strek, opphøyd i annen så avvik i begge retninger teller positivt, summert, delt på n minus én, og til slutt kvadratroten for å komme tilbake til de opprinnelige enhetene.
Så s, i blått, er et typisk avvik fra gjennomsnittet: stort s betyr spredte data, lite s betyr at nesten alt ligger nær x-strek.
Det ene forteller hvor dataene er, det andre hvor mye de sprer seg rundt det stedet.

request: Why does coffee go cold in a mug in an hour but stay hot in a flask all day?
title: The flask that only subtracts

request: What does it actually cost a country to build more hospitals?

spec.title: Economics 1 · What a hospital really costs

commands.speak: A new hospital comes with an invoice. An economist will tell you the invoice is not the cost.
Hospitals along the bottom, and up the side everything else the country makes — schools, roads, pensions, coffee.
This curve is the edge of the possible: every mix on it uses every nurse, builder and machine the country has, with nobody left idle.
Everything in here is possible too, but only by leaving people and machines standing still.
Now what the country wants. Along this line every mix pleases it equally well, and it is the best such line the economy can actually reach.
So this year's budget lands where the two just touch: a few hospitals, and a great deal of everything else.
And here is the question no invoice can answer — what does one more hospital cost from there?
The answer is the steepness of the curve at that point, and up at this end it is nearly flat: the first hospital takes builders who were barely needed elsewhere, so almost nothing else is given up.
Now suppose health becomes the priority, and the country goes on buying hospitals.
Same curve, same country, and the slope where it now sits is steep. One more hospital takes surgeons and steel from schools that genuinely needed them.
Which is why an economist meets every price with the question “compared with what?” Milton Friedman made a book title of the answer: there is no such thing as a free lunch.
The cost of a hospital was never the invoice, then. It is a slope — the schools you no longer build — and it climbs with every hospital you add.

request: If nobody sets the price, how does a market end up with one?

commands.speak: Nobody in this city sets the rent. No committee meets, no minister signs anything — and yet there is a going rate.
Flats to rent along the bottom, the monthly rent up the side.
Tenants first: the cheaper flats are, the more people want one — students who would otherwise share, couples who would otherwise stay put. Demand slopes down.
Landlords read the same number the other way round. The higher the rent, the more flats get built, converted, and let out rather than left empty.
The two lines cross exactly once.
At that rent every tenant willing to pay it finds a flat, and every landlord willing to let at it finds a tenant. Nobody is left holding anything.
That is the one rent in the picture with nothing pushing on it — a claim worth testing, so let us pick a different one.
The city caps the rent below the crossing, meaning well: rents shall not exceed this.
Read across to both curves at the capped rent. Many more tenants now want a flat…
…and fewer landlords are willing to offer one. That gap is a queue: people who would gladly pay the capped rent and find nothing at all.

A queue is pressure. Someone slips the landlord a little extra, a flat goes quietly to a cousin, or it leaves the market as a holiday let. New York has had rent control since a wartime freeze in nineteen forty-three, and its housing queue is a famous institution.
Set the rent above the crossing instead and the pressure runs the other way, with empty flats and landlords cutting deals.

quiz.question: At a rent set above the crossing, what shows up?
quiz.right: Empty flats — landlords offer more than tenants will take at that rent, and every empty month argues the rent back down.
quiz.wrong: Read both curves across at the higher rent: landlords offer more, tenants want fewer.

commands.speak: You answered {score} of {score_total}. So the crossing is not where a market is told to sit — it is the only rent nobody has a reason to move away from, which is how a price gets set by no one in particular.

request: A tax is collected from sellers, so why do buyers end up paying part of it?

spec.title: Economics 3 · Who really pays a tax

commands.speak: A tax on cigarettes is collected from the shop, so why do smokers end up paying part of it? Packs along the bottom, price per pack up the side.
Demand lies flat, because this is a town of casual smokers: if the price moved much, they would quit, or buy in the next town.
Supply rises as always: the better the price, the more shops bother to stock them.
Untaxed, the market settles here.
Now a fixed tax on every pack, paid by the shop. Each pack costs the shop that much more, so the supply curve lifts by exactly the tax.
The new crossing sets the shelf price, and it has not risen by the whole tax: by less than a fifth of it.
Buyers now pay this much, noticeably more than before the tax.
But after paying the tax, the shop keeps only this much.
The band between the two prices, across every pack still sold, is the government's revenue.
The other four fifths come out of the shop's price. With buyers this quick to leave, the seller swallows most of the tax rather than lose them.
And a third thing appears: packs nobody sells any more, though buyers valued them above what sellers would have taken. Nobody collects that. It is simply gone.
England's window tax of 1696 made such a loss visible: people bricked up windows rather than pay, and lived in the dark.
Now the same tax in a town of committed smokers, who buy their packs whatever they cost. Demand steepens.
The shelf price now carries nearly four fifths of the tax. The shop passes on what it can, because these buyers do not leave.
And the lost wedge has shrunk to about a quarter of its size, because few trades were given up. Taxing what people won't give up raises much and wastes little.
What if the shops can walk away too, with shelf space that will happily hold something else?
Then buyers carry about nine tenths of the tax, and the shop barely feels it.
So who pays is not written in the tax law. The tax settles on whichever side finds it harder to walk away.

quiz.question: The same tax is collected from smokers at the till instead of from shops. Who bears more of it?
choices: Smokers now bear all of it
Shops now bear all of it
quiz.right: The split stays the same: buyers and sellers end up facing the same two prices whoever hands over the money, and only how easily each side walks away decides the split.

request: Why does competition leave a firm no profit at all?

commands.speak: Why does competition leave a firm no profit? Take a bakery that opens in a town with none: for a year it prints money, then it stops.
Marginal cost is what one more loaf costs: falling while the ovens fill up, then climbing as the bakers go into overtime.
Average total cost spreads everything over the loaves: flour, wages, rent, the oven. It bottoms out where the bakery is worked just right.
The bakery is too small to move the price of bread, so the market hands it a flat line: 78 cents a loaf.
How much to bake? Keep going while one more loaf sells for more than it costs to make, and stop where marginal cost reaches the price.
There, each loaf costs about 35 cents on average, so about 43 cents of every sale is profit. That rectangle is the total.
Word of a rectangle like that travels.
A second bakery opens, then a third. Together they bake more bread than the town was buying, and the price slides to 40 cents.
Each bakery follows the same rule, bakes a little less, and keeps about 16 cents a loaf.
And newcomers keep arriving while there is anything left to arrive for.
The price comes to rest at the bottom of average cost, and the rectangle is a sliver: under a cent a loaf.
Yet nothing has gone wrong. Average cost already includes a normal return: what the owner's time and money could earn elsewhere.
An accountant would still report a profit. What competition removes is the extra, and it hands that to the customer as cheaper bread.

quiz.question: In the long run, a competitive bakery earns zero economic profit. What does the owner earn?
choices: What her time and money could earn elsewhere
quiz.right: What her time and money could earn elsewhere: that normal return is counted as a cost, so zero economic profit still pays the owner.

request: Where does a recession come from, and what can a government actually do about it?

spec.title: Economics 5 · When the economy falls short

commands.speak: Where does a recession come from? The factories still stand and the workers still know their jobs, yet output falls. Everything produced in a year runs along the bottom.
Aggregate demand is all the spending there is: households, firms, government, foreigners. A lower price level makes money go further and exports cheaper, so more gets bought.
Aggregate supply is what firms produce at each price level. With wages fixed by contract for a while, better prices make them run harder.
Where the two cross is what the economy is doing this year.
This vertical line is what it could produce with everyone who wants a job working: its potential. Just now the two agree.
Lay a second demand curve over the first, and give the economy some bad news.
Firms postpone an investment, households save for a rainy day, an export market closes. Nobody produced less because they could not; nobody ordered it.
That distance is the recession: output below potential, with the factories and workers idle. Economists call it the output gap.
The price level slipped too. A slump of missing spending comes with weak prices, not inflation, and that tells you which medicine it needs.
If what is missing is spending, spending can replace it: a government that cuts taxes or builds something, a central bank that makes borrowing cheap.
Output returns to potential. That argument is John Maynard Keynes's, published in 1936 in the middle of the slump it describes.
On this picture a recession is not an economy that cannot produce. It is one that is not being asked to, and that is a fixable kind of trouble.

quiz.question: A recession opens a gap below potential output. What is missing?
choices: Spending on what the economy can make
quiz.right: Spending. All the capacity is still there, which is why policy that lifts demand can close the gap.
quiz.wrong: Look at what actually moved in the picture: only the demand curve. The supply side never budged.

request: Hvorfor sprekker en boble, når alle vet at prisen er for høy?

commands.speak: En boble er en kjede av kjøpere, og hver av dem regner med det samme.
Kjøper 1 betaler for mye, men det gjør ingenting: kjøper 2 betaler mer.
Kjøper 2 tenker likedan, og kjøper 3 bekrefter regnestykket.
Prisen har ikke lenger noe med verdien å gjøre — den handler bare om neste ledd.
Og kjeden holder akkurat så lenge det finnes et neste ledd, så da det tar slutt, er det kjøper 3 som sitter igjen med regningen.

request: Hvordan blir en lov til i Norge?

commands.speak: En lov begynner som et forslag, fra regjeringen eller fra en representant.
Først går det til en komité, der det leses, høres og skrives om.
Så kommer det i salen, der alle kan si sitt og stemmen telles.
Blir det vedtatt to ganger, er forslaget blitt en lov.
Og det er i komiteen det meste av arbeidet skjer — lenge før noen stemmer.

request: Hva skjer med et søk i en søkemotor?

commands.speak: Hva skjer egentlig når du søker? Nesten alt har skjedd før du trykker enter. Her er nettet, krympet til tre sider.
Et program, en robot, følger lenker fra side til side og henter hver side det finner, døgnet rundt.
Så lages indeksen: for hvert ord, en liste over sidene der ordet står. Som registeret bak i en bok.
Fly står på side én og to, Bergen på én og tre. Hos Google gjelder det hundrevis av milliarder sider.
Først nå skriver du: fly bergen.
Søkemotoren leser ikke nettet nå. Det ville tatt uker.
Den har jo allerede gjort jobben.
Den slår opp de to ordene i indeksen og får to korte lister: én og to, én og tre.
Så rangeres treffene. Side én har begge ordene, og havner øverst.
Side to og tre har bare ett ord hver. Hvem av dem som kommer først, må avgjøres på en annen måte.
Én viktig ledetråd er lenkene: en lenke fra en annen side teller som en stemme for siden.
Den ideen var kjernen i PageRank, som Larry Page og Sergey Brin beskrev i 1998, samme år som Google ble grunnlagt.
Så når svaret kommer på under et sekund, er det fordi det tunge arbeidet ble gjort før du spurte.

quiz.question: Du legger ut en ny nettside i dag. Hvorfor dukker den ikke opp i søk med en gang?
choices: Roboten har ikke hentet og indeksert den ennå
Søkemotoren leter bare i gamle sider
Nye sider må betale for å vises
quiz.right: Roboten har ikke vært der ennå: et søk slår bare opp i indeksen, og siden kommer med først når den er hentet og lagt inn.

request: Hvorfor faller ikke en fallskjermhopper fortere og fortere hele veien ned?

commands.speak: Slipp noe tungt fra stor høyde, og det faller ikke fortere og fortere hele veien ned.
Det finnes én fart der lufta bremser akkurat like hardt som tyngdekraften drar.
I starten øker farten raskt, men jo fortere du faller, jo hardere tar lufta imot — helt til kurven flater ut her.
Helt i begynnelsen er lufta nesten ikke der: det er da du virkelig akselererer.
Og derfor er sluttfarten ikke en grense noen har satt — den er der de to kreftene er like store.

title: A tax's deadweight loss — Haiku 4.5

# How Taxes Create Deadweight Loss

## Supply, Demand, and the Untaxed Market
use: supply_demand
with: {"demand":{"curvature":"linear","label":"D"},"supply":{"label":"S"},"equilibrium":{"show":true,"guides":true,"q_label":"Q₀","p_label":"P₀"},"regions":["consumer_surplus","producer_surplus"]}

In any market, a buyer and seller meet at a price where supply equals demand.
    draw axes

At this point, called equilibrium, the quantity bought and sold is Q₀ at price P₀.
    draw demand_curve label_D

Consumers who were willing to pay more than P₀ gain surplus—the blue triangle above the price.
    draw supply_curve label_S

    pause 0.3

Producers who were willing to sell for less than P₀ gain surplus—the green triangle below the price.
    draw equilibrium_point guide_lines label_E label_Pstar label_Qstar

These two gains together form the total surplus: the entire benefit the market creates.
    draw cs_region label_CS

This is the baseline—no tax yet, no waste.
    draw ps_region label_PS

Every unit that trades at equilibrium creates value for both sides.
    highlight cs_region ps_region effect glow

    pause 0.5

Now imagine the government imposes a tax. What happens?

## The Tax Wedge and Lost Trades
use: supply_demand
with: {"demand":{"curvature":"linear","label":"D"},"supply":{"label":"S"},"equilibrium":{"show":true,"guides":true},"tax":{"amount":18,"side":"seller"},"regions":["consumer_surplus","producer_surplus","deadweight_loss"]}

Now that we have seen the untaxed market, let's add a tax and watch what happens.
    draw axes

    pause 0.3

Demand and supply, the same as before.
    draw demand_curve label_D supply_curve label_S parallel true

And the equilibrium where they cross.
    draw equilibrium_point guide_lines label_E label_Pstar label_Qstar

    pause 0.4

A tax inserts a wedge between what consumers pay and what producers receive.
    draw tax_supply_curve label_S_tax

    pause 0.3

Consumers now face a higher price Pc; producers now receive a lower price Ps.
    draw price_buyers_point price_sellers_point label_Pb label_Ps

    highlight label_Pb label_Ps effect glow

At this new price pair, fewer units are traded—the quantity falls from Q₀ to Q₁.
    draw wedge_region

    pause 0.3

But here is the key: the units between Q₁ and Q₀ were still worth trading.
    point at.ref dwl_region gesture circle

    pause 0.2

Each of these lost units would have created value—someone was willing to buy above Ps, and someone was willing to sell below Pc.

The tax prevents that trade from happening.
    highlight dwl_region effect glow

    pause 0.3

The red zone shows the surplus those ghost trades would have created—but it vanishes.

This vanishing value is deadweight loss: a pure loss to society, gained by no one.
    draw label_DWL

## Non-Linear Growth and a Mathematical Example
Now that we have seen the tax wedge, let's ask: how does the loss grow as the tax gets larger?
    axes axes x_label "Tax rate (t)" y_label "Deadweight loss (DWL)"

The deadweight loss is not proportional to the tax. It is proportional to the tax squared.
    curve dwl_curve #b5482e expr 0.5*x*x/4
    label curve_label "DWL = ½·a·t²" above-right attach_to dwl_curve

    pause 0.4

Suppose demand is Q = 100 − P and supply is Q = P. The equilibrium is Q₀ = 50 at P₀ = 50.

    pause 0.3

A per-unit tax t lowers quantity to Q₁ = 50 − t/2, creating a deadweight loss of exactly DWL = t²/4.

    pause 0.4

When t = 2, the loss is 1. When t = 4, the loss is 4. When t = 6, the loss is 9.
    text row_header "t     DWL" x 650 y 520 font_size 22
    text row_1 "t = 2   DWL = 1" x 650 y 460 font_size 20
    text row_2 "t = 4   DWL = 4" x 650 y 400 font_size 20
    text row_3 "t = 6   DWL = 9" x 650 y 340 font_size 20

Notice: double the tax, quadruple the loss. A small tax of 2 costs society 1 unit of surplus.
    mark highlight_row_1 around row_1 kind box

    pause 0.3

But a tax of 6—only three times larger—costs 9 units, nine times more.
    mark highlight_row_2 around row_2 kind box
    mark highlight_row_3 around row_3 kind box

    pause 0.3

This is why high taxes are so wasteful: each marginal increase in the tax destroys surplus at an accelerating rate.
    highlight dwl_curve effect glow

    pause 0.4

You can now see why governments must balance tax revenue against the waste it creates.

## Synthesis: the Hidden Cost of Taxation

with: {"demand":{"curvature":"linear","label":"D"},"supply":{"label":"S"},"equilibrium":{"show":true,"guides":true},"tax":{"amount":18},"regions":["deadweight_loss"]}

    text tax_var "t = tax amount" x 150 y 680 font_size 20 hidden true
    math formula top-right tex "\\text{DWL} = \\tfrac{1}{2} a \\cdot t^2" size 28 hidden true
    label parabola_label "DWL grows as t²" above attach_to dwl_parabola hidden true

Now that we have seen the supply and demand curves, the tax  (@draw axes demand_curve label_D supply_curve label_S@)wedge, and the mathematics of how deadweight loss grows: a tax always shrinks the market, prevents beneficial trades, and destroys surplus.

    pause 0.3

That destruction is not (@draw equilibrium_point guide_lines@) linear—it accelerates.

    pause 0.3

A 10% tax destroys far more value per percentage point than a 1% tax.
    draw tax_supply_curve label_S_tax tax_equilibrium_point

    pause 0.3

This is not a reason to avoid taxation: governments need revenue, and many taxes are justified.
    draw dwl_region label_DWL

But it is a reason to see taxation clearly: every dollar collected costs society more than a dollar in lost surplus.
    point at.ref dwl_region gesture circle

    pause 0.3

The deadweight loss is the price of public finance.
    draw dwl_parabola parabola_label

Now when you look at a tax policy, you can see not only the revenue it raises, but the trades it kills and the value that evaporates.

That is the hidden arithmetic of taxation.

## The Wedge and the Lost Trades

Every tax on a good does one simple thing: it splits one price into two — what the buyer pays, and what the seller keeps.

Here is a market before any tax: the upward supply curve S, the downward demand curve D, crossing at price P0 and quantity Q0.

That crossing point is where every trade that helps both sides actually happens — nobody who would gain from trading is left out.

Quantity falls from Q0 to Q1, because at the new prices fewer trades clear both sides at once.

The government collects tax revenue equal to t times Q1 — that shaded rectangle.
    draw wedge_region label_wedge

Next, we ask what happens to that triangle as the tax grows.
    point at.ref dwl_region gesture underline

## Loss Grows Faster Than the Tax

Double the tax to t2, and two things happen at once.

Now that we know the loss grows with the square of the tax, here is a case where we can compute it exactly.
    card title "A Formula You Can Compute" style center

Take a demand curve P = 10 − Q and a supply curve P = Q — nothing exotic, just two straight lines.
    draw eq_demand eq_supply parallel true

Without any tax they cross at Q0 = 5 and P0 = 5: that is the untaxed equilibrium.
    draw eq_eq0

Put a tax t between buyer and seller: the buyer pays Pb = 10 − Q1, the seller receives Ps = Q1, and Pb − Ps = t.
    draw eq_tax_setup

Solving that gives the new quantity: Q1 = (10 − t) / 2.
    draw eq_q1

The deadweight loss is the triangle's area: one half times its height t times its base, Q0 minus Q1.
    draw eq_dwl_formula

Substitute Q1 in, and the algebra collapses to a strikingly simple result: DWL = t² / 4.
    morph eq_dwl_formula tex "DWL = \\frac{t^2}{4}"

A one-dollar tax costs a quarter of a dollar in lost value; a two-dollar tax costs a full dollar — four times as much for twice the tax.
    draw eq_example

Plot DWL against t and you get a parabola, not a line — the curve itself is the proof of what we saw in the last part.
    draw curve_dwl label_curve point_t1 label_t1 point_t2 label_t2

That is the whole arc: a tax splits one price into two, the gap between them cancels trades that would have paid off, and because both sides of that lost region grow with the tax, the loss itself compounds — visible now as the widening curve on this page.
