request: Why do bridges come in so many different shapes?

commands.speak: Every bridge has the same job: carry a load across a gap without breaking. The shapes differ because materials break in different ways. Start with the simplest: a plank laid across two piers.
Load the middle and it sags. The top of the plank is squeezed — that is compression, in blue — and the underside is stretched — tension, in red.
Stone takes a squeeze well but cracks when stretched, so a stone beam can only ever be short.
The Romans' answer was to curve the load into an arch.
Now every stone is pushed against its neighbours and none is pulled apart. All blue — exactly what stone is good at.
Iron and steel handle both kinds of force, so engineers could return to a straight beam — built as triangles.
The top chord is squeezed and the bottom chord stretched, just like the plank, but with most of the material taken out; the diagonals alternate between the two.
Go further and hang the road from a cable slung between two towers.
The cable only pulls, which steel wire does better than anything, and the towers only push. That split is how the Golden Gate's main span reaches more than twelve hundred metres.
The cable-stayed bridge runs straight cables from a tower down to the deck.
The stays pull, the tower pushes — and because every stay tugs the deck towards the tower, the deck itself is squeezed. France's Millau Viaduct, the tallest bridge in the world, is built this way.
Now put all five side by side. Every design sends part of the load through something that is squeezed.
And all but one pair it with something stretched. The arch has no red at all.
Those two are mirror images. Robert Hooke put it in 1675: as a hanging chain hangs, so, turned upside down, the rigid arch will stand.

quiz.question: Which of the five uses no tension at all?
quiz.right: The arch — curving the load means every stone is squeezed and none is stretched.
quiz.wrong: That one has red in it — something is stretched. Look for the bridge with only blue.

request: Why are floor tiles squares or hexagons, but never pentagons?

spec.title: Which shapes can tile a floor?

card.title: Which shapes can tile a floor?

commands.speak: Bathroom floors use squares and honeycombs use hexagons. Nobody tiles a floor with regular pentagons. Why not? Wherever tiles meet at a corner, their angles must add up to one full turn, 360 degrees. A triangle's corner is 60, and six of them close the circle exactly.
A square's corner is 90: four of them fit.
A pentagon's corner is 108. Three make 324 and leave a gap; four would overlap. No floor.
A hexagon's corner is 120, and three fit exactly.
Seven sides give about 128.6 degrees: two corners are too few, three too many.
Eight give 135 — the same problem, which is why an octagon floor always needs little squares in the gaps.

Now all six together. Only three regular shapes tile a floor on their own, because only 60, 90 and 120 go into 360 a whole number of times. Past six sides every corner is wider than 120, so no whole number of them can make a full turn.
And of those three, the hexagon walls off an area with the least edge. Thomas Hales proved it in 1999; bees had been saving wax that way for millions of years.

quiz.question: Why can't regular pentagons tile a floor?
choices: They have an odd number of sides
quiz.right: Three corners make 324° and four make 432° — no whole number of them makes a full turn.
quiz.wrong: Triangles have an odd number of sides and tile perfectly; it is the corner angle that decides.

request: Why does gravity rule the universe if it's the weakest force?

elements.text: light, chemistry, the push of a hand
turns protons into neutrons in the Sun
the weakest of all, and it only attracts

commands.speak: Physicists count just four forces behind everything that happens. Here they are, strongest first. The strong force holds the nucleus together, against the protons' electric push. It is the strongest, but it reaches barely across one nucleus — orange marks a short reach.
Electromagnetism is light, every chemical bond, and the reason your hand does not pass through a table. Purple: it reaches without limit.
The weak force can turn one particle into another. Without it the Sun could not start fusing: its first step turns a proton into a neutron.
And gravity — so feeble that a fridge magnet beats the pull of the whole Earth. Next to the strong force it is weaker by a factor of ten to the thirty-eight.
So why does the weakest force hold planets in orbit and whole galaxies together?
The two strong ones reach no further than a nucleus, so beyond an atom they simply vanish.

Of the two with endless reach, electric charges come as plus and minus and cancel, so a planet is almost perfectly neutral. Mass only ever adds up. Pile up a planet's worth, and the weakest force is the only one left pulling.

quiz.question: Why does gravity, the weakest force, dominate the motion of planets?
choices: It only attracts, so it adds up
It is strongest at long distances
quiz.right: Charges cancel and the nuclear forces stop at the nucleus, but mass only adds up — so on a planet's scale gravity is what is left.
quiz.wrong: Gravity is not stronger far away. What matters is that it never cancels: mass only adds up.

request: How long does each kind of note last in music?

spec.title: Five shapes, each half the last

card.title: Five shapes, each half the last

commands.speak: Before a note tells you its pitch, its shape tells you how long to hold it. Five shapes do most of the work. The whole note: an open oval, held for four beats — a full bar of ordinary four-four time.
Give it a stem and it lasts half as long: two beats.
Fill the head in, and halve it again: one beat, the one you tap your foot to.
A flag on the stem halves it once more: half a beat.
Two flags, a quarter of a beat. Every new mark says the same thing: halve it.
So one whole note lasts as long as sixteen of these.
Oddly, the British still call the whole note a semibreve — half a short note. Medieval music had longer notes still, and this one was once the short one.

quiz.question: In four-four time, which note lasts exactly one beat?
quiz.right: The quarter note — a filled head on a stem, one beat.
quiz.wrong: Count the halvings from the whole note's four beats: half is two, quarter is one.

request: Why doesn't the Moon fall down onto the Earth?

spec.title: Why doesn't the Moon fall down?

card.title: Why doesn't the Moon fall down?

commands.speak: The Moon is falling towards the Earth right now. Newton worked out why it never lands, with an imaginary cannon. Put a cannon on a mountain so tall it pokes above the air, and fire it sideways.
A gentle shot curves down and lands close by.
Fire harder and it lands farther away — and by now the ground has begun to curve away beneath it.
At about eight kilometres a second, the ground curves away exactly as fast as the ball falls. It falls forever and never lands: an orbit.
Faster still, past eleven kilometres a second, and it falls too slowly ever to come back.
Every orbit lies between these two — the Moon's, and the space station's, which is falling around the Earth at nearly eight kilometres a second.
So the Moon does fall. It is just moving sideways fast enough to keep missing.

quiz.question: Why doesn't the Moon crash into the Earth?
choices: It moves sideways fast enough to keep missing
quiz.right: It falls all the time, but its sideways speed carries it past the curve of the Earth before it can land.
quiz.wrong: Gravity reaches the Moon — that is why it curves at all. It keeps missing because it moves sideways so fast.

request: How do the two hands share a piano score?

params.notes: E4:q E4:q F4:q G4:q G4:q F4:q E4:q D4:q

commands.speak: A piano has one keyboard, but its music is written on two staves at once. Why two? The top staff, with the treble clef, is for the higher notes — mostly the right hand.
The bottom staff, with the bass clef, is for the low notes — the left hand. The brace says: read these two together.

commands.play: E4:q E4:q F4:q G4:q G4:q F4:q E4:q D4:q
commands.speak: The right hand plays the tune.
The left hand holds long, low notes underneath.
Notes stacked straight above one another are played at the same moment — that is why the two staves line up by beat.

play.notes: E4:q E4:q F4:q G4:q G4:q F4:q E4:q D4:q

commands.speak: Both hands together.
One staff alone could not hold both: the tune and the bass lie more than an octave apart, and would need a ladder of extra lines between them.

quiz.question: Which staff holds the left hand's low notes?
choices: The top one, with the treble clef
The bottom one, with the bass clef
quiz.right: The bottom staff: the bass clef marks the low notes, usually the left hand.
quiz.wrong: The treble clef is for the high notes. Low notes go on the bass staff below.

request: Can I write the end of a melody myself?

commands.speak: Every melody is a question and an answer. I'll ask the question; you write the answer. A staff, and a keyboard under it: each line and space of the staff is one white key.
Four notes climbing, one step at a time — it sounds unfinished, like a question.
Your turn. Click the staff to the right of my notes, or press the keys, and write four notes that sound like an answer. Try ending on C. Then press Continue.
Here is the whole line, question and answer.
A tune that comes home to the note it started from sounds finished — that pull back to C is what musicians call the tonic.

request: How do musicians hear where a note goes on the staff?

spec.title: Can you hear where a note goes?

card.title: Can you hear where a note goes?

commands.speak: Musicians can often write down a tune they hear. It starts with one skill: hearing how high a note is. Higher notes sit higher on the staff; lower notes lower. Each step up is one line or one space.
This is middle C, on its own little line under the staff.
And this is G — five steps higher, and it sounds it.
Now just listen.

ask.question: Where does that note go? Click it on the staff.
ask.right: E — the bottom line, between the C and the G.
ask.wrong: It was E, on the bottom line: higher than C, lower than G.

commands.speak: Five more, and you choose. Press the speaker to hear a note again.
You placed {ears} of {ears.total}. Every musician's ear is trained exactly this way — one note at a time.

request: Why do cellos and tubas read a different clef?

params.notes: C2:q E2:q G2:q C3:q E3:q G3:q C4:h

commands.speak: A cello or a tuba plays notes far below the treble staff. Written there, they would hang from a ladder of extra lines. So low instruments use the bass clef. Its two dots sit either side of the fourth line: that line is F, below middle C.
Up a C major chord, from deep C to middle C — every note sits comfortably on the staff.
And middle C, at the top, is the same note the treble staff writes on a ledger line below it — the two staves meet there.
The clefs are letters in disguise: the treble clef is a curly G, and this one is an old-fashioned F.

quiz.question: Which letter does the bass clef's line mark?
quiz.right: F — the two dots surround the F line, below middle C.
quiz.wrong: The treble clef marks G. The bass clef's two dots surround F.

request: What do the two numbers at the start of a piece of music mean?

commands.speak: At the start of almost every piece of music sit two stacked numbers. They tell you how to feel the beat before you hear a note. Four over four: four beats in every bar, each a quarter note long. Count it: one, two, three, four.

commands.play: C3:q E4+G4:q C3:q E4+G4:q C3:q E4+G4:q C3:q E4+G4:q
commands.speak: A march — left, right, left, right.
Change the top number to three, and every bar has three beats.

commands.play: C3:q E4+G4:q E4+G4:q C3:q E4+G4:q E4+G4:q
commands.speak: Now it sways: ONE two three, ONE two three. That is a waltz.
Sometimes four-four is written as a C. It looks like C for common time — but it is really a broken circle from medieval music, where a full circle meant three beats and a broken one meant two.
The top number counts the beats in a bar; the bottom one says which note gets one beat.

quiz.question: Which time signature makes a waltz?
quiz.right: Three-four: three beats a bar — ONE two three.
quiz.wrong: A waltz sways in threes: three-four, three beats in every bar.

request: How do I read the notes on the treble staff?

params.notes: E4:q G4:q B4:q D5:q F5:q F4:q A4:q C5:q E5:q

commands.speak: Reading music feels like a secret code. For the treble staff, two short sentences are the whole key. The treble clef curls around the second line from the bottom — that line is G, which is why the clef is also called the G clef.
Now the five lines, from the bottom up.
E, G, B, D, F — Every Good Boy Deserves Fruit.
And the four spaces between them.
F, A, C, E — the spaces spell a word: FACE.
Your turn: find five notes on the staff. Say the sentences under your breath.
You found {read} of {read.total}. Two sentences, and every note on the staff has a name.

request: What do the sharp, flat and natural signs do in music?

commands.speak: Three small signs in front of a note change it. Listen to what each one does. A sharp raises a note by the smallest step on a piano — from C to the black key just above it.
A flat lowers it by the same half step — E down to the black key below.
And a natural cancels either one: the note goes back to its white key.
The shapes are old. Medieval scribes wrote B two ways: a round b for the low B, a square one for the high B — the round b became the flat, the square one the natural and the sharp.

quiz.question: A sharp in front of C sends you to…
choices: the black key just above C
the black key just below C
quiz.right: The black key just above C — a sharp raises by a half step, the smallest step on a piano.
quiz.wrong: A sharp raises by a half step: the very next key up, which from C is the black key.
